articles.title: Orange et Free cités parmi les meilleurs réseaux 5G du monde dans une prestigieuse étude
articles.text:
Le classement mondial 5G d'Opensignal pour 2026, publié mardi, place deux opérateurs français aux avant-postes. Orange s'illustre sur le débit, Free sur la fiabilité, tandis que SFR et Bouygues Telecom ne décrochent aucune distinction.
Opensignal a publié ses 5G Global Awards 2026, un palmarès établi à partir de milliards de mesures réalisées sur les smartphones des utilisateurs entre le 1er janvier et le 29 juin. Sept critères ont été passés au peigne fin, et au bout du compte, la société indépendante d'analyse mobile a rendu ce mardi 29 septembre un verdict qui laisse peu de place au chauvinisme. La France ne remporte aucune catégorie, même si l'opérateur historique, Orange, s'invite parmi les réseaux 5G les plus rapides de sa catégorie, et Free parmi les plus fiables au monde. Ailleurs, nos opérateurs frôlent parfois les lauréats à quelques dixièmes de point près, ce qui rend la lecture du palmarès assez intéressante.
Orange fonce et Free tient bon : la 5G française a ses têtes d'affiche
Commençons par la vitesse. Opensignal a fait le choix de répartir les pays en deux groupes selon leur superficie, et la France concourt dans la cour des grands, face aux États-Unis, au Brésil ou à l'Allemagne. Avec 280,3 Mbit/s de débit descendant (vitesse en téléchargement) en 5G, Orange s'y classe 9e et décroche le titre de « 5G Global Leader ». C'est le Brésilien Vivo qui trône en tête, avec 44 Mbit/s d'avance sur l'opérateur français.
Le résultat est d'autant plus flatteur qu'aucun opérateur n'apparaît dans le top 20 en Allemagne, en Espagne ou en Italie. Seul T-Mobile, mais non pas en Allemagne mais en Pologne, figure parmi les leaders, tandis que l'Espagnol DIGI pointe au 12e rang (266,4 Mbit/s). Aucun Français n'est en revanche parmi les quinze plus fortes accélérations de l'année, un classement écrasé par le Péruvien Bitel et son bond de 226,9 Mbit/s.
Free, de son côté, se distingue sur un terrain moins spectaculaire peut-être, mais tout aussi précieux, peut-être plus même, à savoir la fiabilité. Avec 970,3 points sur une échelle de 100 à 1 000, il décroche lui aussi un titre de leader, de justesse, puisqu'il est 11e sur les 12 opérateurs distingués. Les Japonais au (981,4) et SoftBank (980,5) s'emparent de la victoire, tandis qu'Orange talonne Free, 16e avec 967,7 points.
En vidéo, Orange et Bouygues Telecom ne déméritent pas, SFR absent
Sur la vidéo en 5G, ça se joue à un cheveu. Opensignal y a sacré douze lauréats, sans décerner le moindre titre de leader. Le dernier d'entre eux, le Finlandais Telia, affiche 78,3 points sur 100. Orange (78) et Bouygues Telecom (77,9), 17e et 18e, pointent à trois et quatre dixièmes de lui. Orange Pologne figure, lui, parmi les heureux élus, avec 78,5 points.
Ailleurs, le bilan est plus timide. Aucun opérateur de l'Hexagone ne se hisse dans le top 20 de la couverture 5G, menée par T-Mobile USA (8,4 sur 10). Aucun non plus parmi les distingués du jeu mobile ou du temps passé en 5G, nouvel indicateur de cette édition. Sur les appels passés par des applications de type WhatsApp ou autres, Orange affiche l'une des quinze plus fortes progressions annuelles (+2,7 points, 12e ex æquo). C'est encore trop peu pour rejoindre les cinq « Rising Stars » de la catégorie.
Et SFR, dans tout ça ? Contrairement à certains opérateurs étrangers écartés faute d'une 5G assez étendue, l'opérateur au carré rouge a d'après nos constatations bien été retenu dans l'analyse d'Opensignal, mais il repart sans la moindre distinction. De quoi mesurer le chemin à parcourir pour lui. La Finlande rafle douze récompenses avec trois opérateurs, et Deutsche Telekom en cumule quatre, dont une victoire sur le jeu mobile. La 5G française tient son rang et fait assez bonne figure, sans que l'on puisse toutefois dire qu'elle domine la concurrence.

articles.title: La nouvelle Garmin Forerunner 70, idéale pour débuter la course à pied, voit déjà son prix baisser — Frandroid
articles.text:
Lancée en mai 2026 aux côtés de la Forerunner 170, la Forerunner 70 prend la relève de la Forerunner 55. Le changement le plus visible concerne l’écran. L’ancienne dalle MIP transflective laisse place à un écran AMOLED tactile, une nouveauté sur ce segment chez Garmin. La montre reprend aussi des fonctions d’entraînement qui étaient jusqu’ici réservées aux modèles plus chers. Si vous cherchez une première montre GPS pour vous mettre à courir, elle est en ce moment disponible pour 229 euros.
La Garmin Forerunner 70, c’est quoi ?
- Un écran AMOLED tactile de 1,2 pouce en 390 x 390 pixels
- Des fonctionnalités orientées sport
- Jusqu’à 13 jours d’autonomie en mode montre connectée
Lancée à 249 euros, la Garmin Forerunner 70 perd 20 euros sur Amazon, où elle est affichée à 229 euros.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant la Garmin Forerunner 70. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un écran AMOLED dans un boîtier de 40 g
Jusqu’ici, la porte d’entrée incontournable dans l’univers des montres de sport Garmin était la Forerunner 55. Avec l’arrivée de la Forerunner 70, la marque modernise sa formule et propose un bond en avant sur la partie affichage. Exit l’ancien écran MIP : la nouvelle venue adopte une dalle tactile AMOLED de 1,2 pouce avec une définition de 390 x 390 pixels. Résultat, les couleurs flattent la rétine et l’arrivée du tactile simplifie au passage la navigation dans les menus au quotidien, sans pour autant sacrifier les boutons physiques, bien pratiques pour lancer une activité.
Avec son boîtier plutôt compact de 42,6 mm et son poids plume de seulement 40 grammes, la montre se fait presque oublier une fois au poignet. C’est un vrai plus si vous aimez suivre la qualité de votre sommeil sans être gêné la nuit. Côté robustesse, elle n’est pas fragile pour autant : son verre renforcé résiste bien aux petits chocs du quotidien, et avec son étanchéité 5 ATM, vous pouvez la garder sans stress sous la douche ou pour faire quelques longueurs à la piscine.
Un coach qui s’adapte à votre forme
La montre est capable de mesurer votre fréquence cardiaque en continu et dispose d’un oxymètre de pouls pour surveiller l’oxygène sanguin, mais aussi votre niveau de stress ou encore l’énergie de votre Body Battery. La nuit, elle analyse votre sommeil dans le détail — score dédié, détection des siestes et conseils de récupération compris. Elle mesure également la variabilité de la fréquence cardiaque (VFC) pendant votre repos, un indicateur idéal pour savoir si votre corps est prêt à remettre un coup d’accélérateur ou s’il vaut mieux lever le pied.
La Garmin Forerunner 70 monte d’un cran en piquant des fonctions aux modèles haut de gamme. Elle adapte vos entraînements au quotidien selon votre forme, inclut les plans gratuits Garmin Coach et mesure même la puissance de course au poignet (cadence, temps de contact au sol). Avec ses 80 profils sportifs — de la course à la natation en passant par la muscu —, c’est un vrai couteau suisse pour progresser.
Côté endurance, Garmin promet jusqu’à 13 jours d’autonomie (et 23h en suivi GPS), même s’il faudra revoir ce chiffre à la baisse si vous gardez l’écran AMOLED toujours allumé. Autre concession : l’absence de GPS double fréquence, qui peut rendre le tracé un poil moins précis sous les arbres ou entre de grands immeubles.
Si vous souhaitez la comparer à d’autres modèles de course ou de sport, jetez un œil à notre guide des meilleures montres connectées.

articles.title: Trump Says Top Tech Firms Have Signed Accord to ‘Self-Police’ AI Development
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews during a meeting at the White House aimed at addressing Americans’ fears about the technology.
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson met with leading executives from top tech firms that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centers in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition.
The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX.
The accord, which Trump posted on his social media site, Truth Social, late Tuesday, opened the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take.
The accord said the companies would implement “robust internal controls,” partner with an “independent external auditor” to assess whether the controls were working, and establish a committee within each company’s board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors.
“Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said.
Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce “unbelievable growth.” Investment in data centers and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending.
Yet there were some notes of caution Tuesday. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voicescalling for a slowdown in AI development, said, “The technology has very real risks.”
“And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion,” Amodei said.
Putting faith in ‘self-policing’ AI
Trump suggested that about 10 people would be named to a committee to “watch over the whole enterprise” and said the accord would be “morally binding.” He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry.
Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures these companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing.
The intention of the accord balances the latitude needed for innovation with regulation, said Shri Narayanan, a university professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Southern California. That innovation is not just limited to improving the capabilities of these AI models, Narayanan said, but also to efforts to improve model safety and security.
Other experts are skeptical of putting “so much faith in self-policing,” like Robin Jia, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Southern California. Jia said it’s crucial to ensure the leading labs’ intentions are “well-aligned with the broader interest of the American public.” He pointed to the recent disclosures of hacking incidents and said: “As the models get better, the consequences of such things are only going to get greater.”
Some also took issue with the accord’s vague, broad language. Alex Pascal, executive director of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, said: “The only way to reduce the risks and harms of AI to Americans is through robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers whose costs are borne by the American people.”
Trump unveils chatbot to help Americans navigate government service
Huang sat to Trump’s right during a White House luncheon meeting, according to a seating chart the president posted on Truth Social. Musk sat to Trump’s left.
Earlier Tuesday, Trump promised that the U.S. government wouldn’t limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for “guardrails” or other restrictions.
“I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. “We can’t stifle it, and we’re leading by a lot.”
The unveiling of the AI government chatbot occurred at a daylong event in Washington during which multiple Trump administration officials celebrated a “Golden Age” fueled by what Trump insists on calling “super intelligence,” rather than artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio highlighted that the chatbot at America.gov could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online, without the in-person visit to a processing center currently required.
Trump thinks data centers are going to become ‘very popular’
Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centers cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
“You’re going to see, data centers are going to be very popular,” Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, “they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations.”
Also Tuesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a television interview that the company is increasingly focused on safety. The day before, his company halted the rollout of a new model over safety concerns.
“We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model,” he said on CNBC. “We have to do these in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don’t have a bunch of anxiety.”
For his part, Trump on Tuesday portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no “second place.”
The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. But Trump underscored Tuesday that he didn’t want to cooperate too much with China: “I didn’t want to do anything, because we’re leading. Why would I want to do anything?”

Related: OpenAI Says Its Models Engaged With US Gov Websites in Model Misbehavior Disclosure
Related: Autonomous AI Hacks Raise Thorny Questions of Legal Accountability

articles.title: How Lagos yellow buses became the star of a Nigerian video game
articles.text:
Swipe to the left to dodge the car ahead. Swipe to the right to swerve around a heap of tyres blocking the road. Hit the brake as you approach the yellow-lined bus stop. Passengers tumble out, new ones climb in, and you hit the gas to keep going. A 3D figure carrying a tray steps into the road, so you hit the horn and the familiar pom-pom-pom rings out.
This is Lagos Run, a browser-based endless runner that has taken over Nigerian social media timelines over the past two days. Built by Opeyemi Adeniran, a Berlin-based senior frontend engineer who posts on X as Eureka, the game has drawn more than 20,000 players within two days of its public release, according to him.
Like most endless-runner games, the rules are simple. Players use swipe gestures to steer a danfo, the yellow, black-lined public buses particular to Lagos, Nigeria’s most populous city, collecting coins and boosters along the way. Players must pull over at bus stops to drop off and pick up passengers, dodge other vehicles and pedestrians crossing the road, swerve around roadblocks, and navigate the traffic without crashing.
There are road signs, missions and levels to complete, a leaderboard to compete on, and a radio playing in the background. The result is a digital Lagos, rooted in Ojuelegba, a suburb where Adeniran grew up.
Bringing Lagos to Berlin
Adeniran told TechCabal in an interview on Tuesday that he spent much of his early life around Lagos, where he developed an interest in games. He said he still plays regularly, with Call of Duty Warzone, FIFA, and mobile games like Candy Crush in his rotation.
“I play games almost every day of my life,” he said.
He recalled that he first encountered t game development at the beginning of his career as a frontend engineer in 2017. Since then, he has experimented with different tools, including Unity, a game development software, while exploring ways to build games on the web.
The idea for Lagos Run came after he moved to Germany, and it started partly to explore what was possible with game development.
“I missed home. I needed to go home, so I asked, ‘Why don’t I bring home to myself?’,” he said. “It all started as a side project, but at the moment I see a big picture around it.”
Getting to the version now being played by thousands of people took several attempts, according to Adeniran. He explained that the first version was a flatter, two-dimensional visual experience, different from the current 3D experience users use. The radio feature was not in the original plan, he said, emerging from an attempt to recreate the familiar experience of riding in a danfo inside the virtual version of Lagos.
“When you are in danfo, you usually hear these guys playing radios…,” he said. “So, why don’t we bring the same experience you get when inside danfo into the game as well?”
From the point of coding to the current versions on players’ screens, Adeniran estimates that it took about four to five weeks to build.
Lagos Run currently requires no login or sign-up. The only information players provide is a non-identifying username for the leaderboard. The game has no paywalls; however, Adeniran noted that it has commercial potential.
AI made the build faster
Adeniran told TechCabal that he used artificial intelligence, which has become common in software development. A 2025 study by Game Oracle, a market research platform for indie game developers, found that 20.9% of the 16,554 games released between January 2025 and November 2025 included an AI disclosure statement identifying where and how generative AI tools were used in development. Adeniran said he used AI-generated graphics for the game’s visual assets and Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant, during game development.
“If I were to create this game four, five years ago, it would have taken me months,” he said, “but with AI, anyone could spin up something to work on.”
That faster development cycle could matter in Nigeria’s growing gaming industry. Nigeria’s gaming revenue is forecast to reach $226.6 million in 2026, while mobile gaming accounts for the largest share of Africa’s gaming market. Adeniran argued that AI could help close the gap between the number of ideas developers have and the number of games they can build.
“If we have more people creating stuff and more people testing it out for us and giving us feedback, it would encourage investors to come in and put in some money,” he said.
Lagos Run already provides a small test of that audience. Players on social media began sharing their scores online, challenging friends and comparing themselves on the leaderboard. Some have also suggested new features, prompting Adeniran to set up a WhatsApp channel where players can contribute ideas.
“This is my first time playing a Nigerian-made game,” Ola Lateef, a player who scored over 800,000 points in Lagos Run, said. “It was new, funny, and had a variety of music on the radio. Trending songs, to be specific. I mean, it was very different and enjoyable.”
The attention has also given Adeniran ideas for what could come next. He said he has more games in mind, all rooted in what it feels like to live in Lagos and what people experience there. For Lagos Run itself, the plan is to keep iterating. He is working through bug fixes, new features, and possible collaborations, and taking suggestions from the WhatsApp channel he set up for players.
“When I created the project, it was intended as a side project and for me to see what’s possible around this game development, around this idea I have,” he said. “I feel grateful for the love Nigerians have for helping their people.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Claude Opus 5.5 vs. Fable 5.1: One overthinks, the other cuts corners
articles.text:
Claude Opus 5.5 vs. Fable 5.1: One overthinks, the other cuts corners
Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, saying it performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work. At list price, it costs well under half as much per token. It leads Fable 5.1 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode, and CursorBench. Anthropic says the gap between the two models “is narrower than these scores suggest.” Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 costs $10 and $50.
Anthropic’s own model docs still point developers to Fable 5.1 for “demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work” and list it as the slower of the two. So I wanted to answer two questions in my Opus 5.5 vs. Fable 5.1 testing.
- Is Opus 5.5 really as accurate as Fable 5.1?
- If so, should Fable 5.1 still be sold as the premium model on tasks Opus 5.5 does better?
This is my third Opus 5.5 test. In the first, it matched Opus 5 on reasoning problems at a lower cost, but its speed gain fell short of Anthropic’s claim. This time I focused on coding, where Anthropic’s benchmarks show Opus 5.5 ahead of Fable 5.1.
The tests
I called both models through the Anthropic API with identical prompts, adaptive thinking, and the maximum effort setting. Each test ran five times per model. A hidden test suite graded every test, and I logged tokens, list-price cost, and wall-clock time for every run.
- Agentic bug fix – The model gets a small Python order-pricing repo with four planted bugs and one flaky test, plus tools to list files, read files, write files, and run tests. A hidden suite of 12 tests checks the fixes, and I tracked whether the model touched the tests or noticed the flaky one.
- Resolver spec – The model writes a dependency resolver for a fictional package manager from a two-page spec, without running any code. A hidden suite of 120 tests grades it.
- Concurrency bugs – The model gets an asyncio job queue with three race conditions and an incident report describing double charges and jobs that never ran. It has to find and fix every bug without running the code, and pass eight hidden tests with a controlled clock that checks each fix.
The resolver and concurrency tests each gave the model one prompt and one reply. I started at 64,000, but Opus 5.5 ran out of room, so I raised the limit to 128,000, the maximum either model allows. Fable 5.1 never used more than 55,000.
I didn’t include the prompts here because each test depends on a code repo, spec, or module too long to reprint.
Agentic bug fix
Both models fixed all four bugs in all five runs and passed all 12 hidden tests. Neither one edited the test files, and both flagged the flaky test.
By score alone, the two models tied, but they handled the flaky test differently. The test fails at random because the code simulates a slow call to a shipping carrier’s API. Fable 5.1 “cheated” and deleted the simulated delay in all five runs, so the test always passes. In a real codebase, that would mean removing the API call to make a test pass, and orders would never actually be checked with the carrier. In production, that could mean taking payment for orders the carrier can’t deliver, shipping to addresses it doesn’t serve, and never finding out when its service goes down.
Opus 5.5 left the code alone in all five runs. It confirmed the test was flaky by rerunning it, said shrinking the delay “would just make the test pass without fixing anything,” and pointed to the real fix in the test itself. That’s the better result because the app still works and the developer knows what to fix. A green test suite that hides a broken integration is worse than a red one that tells the truth.
A green test suite that hides a broken integration is worse than a red one that tells the truth.
Opus 5.5 averaged 3 minutes 21 seconds, 25 tool calls, 20,625 output tokens, and $0.75 per run. Fable 5.1 averaged 2 minutes 37 seconds, 22 tool calls, 11,381 output tokens, and $1.50. Opus 5.5 ran the test suite about seven times per run, compared to Fable 5.1’s three, mostly to check the flaky test.
Opus 5.5 won this test, since it fixed the same four bugs as Fable 5.1, handled the flaky test the right way, and cost half as much.
Resolver spec
Both models passed all 120 hidden tests on all five runs.
Opus 5.5 averaged 9 minutes 40 seconds, 70,687 output tokens, and $1.42 per run. Fable 5.1 averaged 6 minutes 46 seconds, 38,710 output tokens, and $1.96. Opus 5.5 used 83% more tokens and still cost 28% less, because each token costs 60% less.
The extra tokens didn’t turn into extra code. Both models wrote about 400 lines, so almost all of Opus 5.5’s extra went into thinking. In one run, Opus 5.5 also opened by listing the places where the spec was unclear and which choice it made for each, something Fable 5.1 never did.
This test was a tie on accuracy, so the winner depends on what you’re optimizing for. Opus 5.5 wins if cost matters most, and Fable 5.1 wins if you need a faster answer.
Concurrency bugs
This test produced the only misses. Fable 5.1 fixed all three race conditions and passed all eight hidden tests on every run.
Opus 5.5 did the same on three runs. On the other two, it used all 128,000 output tokens, then never finished an answer. Each run took about 19 minutes and cost $2.57.
Both models also “fixed” more bugs than I planted. Fable 5.1 listed four to seven fixes per run, and Opus 5.5 listed seven or eight. None of the extra changes broke anything, and some tighten real weak spots, but they mean more code for a reviewer to check.
Opus 5.5 averaged 16 minutes 43 seconds, 111,428 output tokens, and $2.24 per run, counting the failures. Fable 5.1 averaged 8 minutes 27 seconds, 43,001 output tokens, and $2.17. Even on its three finished runs, Opus 5.5 averaged 15 minutes, nearly twice Fable 5.1’s time, and 100,380 tokens, more than twice what Fable 5.1 needed.
Fable 5.1 won this test clearly. It was perfect every time, twice as fast, and cost about the same, because Opus 5.5’s cheaper tokens didn’t make up for using so many more.
Results
| Test (5 runs each) | Opus 5.5 | Fable 5.1 | 
| Agentic bug fix | 5/5 perfect, 3:21, 20,625 out, 25 tool calls, $0.75 | 5/5 perfect, 2:37, 11,381 out, 22 tool calls, $1.50 | 
| Resolver spec | 5/5 perfect, 9:40, 70,687 out, $1.42 | 5/5 perfect, 6:46, 38,710 out, $1.96 | 
| Concurrency bugs | 3/5 perfect, 16:43, 111,428 out, $2.24 | 5/5 perfect, 8:27, 43,001 out, $2.17 | 
| Perfect runs | 13 of 15 | 15 of 15 | 
| Total time, 15 runs | 2:28:39 | 1:29:14 | 
| Total cost, 15 runs | $22.07 | $28.14 | 
Fable 5.1 had 15 perfect runs out of 15, and Opus 5.5 had 13, but the scores don’t tell the whole story. Opus 5.5 won the agentic test by fixing the same bugs without gaming the flaky test, for half the cost. The resolver tied on accuracy. Fable 5.1 won the concurrency test outright, since Opus 5.5 ran out of room twice and returned nothing.
Overall, Opus 5.5 cost 22% less ($22.07 vs. Fable 5.1’s $28.14), but it wrote 2.2 times as many output tokens and took 67% longer to finish all 15 runs.
What do I think?
Of all the tests I’ve done, this one is the hardest “What do I think” section to fill out. Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 are equally flawed, just in different ways. In my opinion, neither should be billed as premium.
Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 are equally flawed, just in different ways.
Opus 5.5 overthinks. It got every run it finished right, but it needed about twice the tokens of Fable 5.1, so it ended up only 22% cheaper, and it hit the token max twice on the hardest test and didn’t produce a result.
Fable 5.1 cuts corners. It never failed a hidden test and was faster on every test, but it passed the agentic test by removing code the app needs.
The premium buys speed and fewer dead ends, not better judgment.
Anthropic is right that Opus 5.5 matches Fable 5.1 on accuracy when it finishes. The premium buys speed and fewer dead ends, not better judgment.
Use Opus 5.5 for agent work, where it can run tests and check itself. Use Fable 5.1 for hard problems it has to solve in one go, or when speed matters. With either one, check what it changed to pass the tests.

articles.title: Cloudflare to become a public certificate authority with post-quantum certificates - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Cloudflare to become a public certificate authority with post-quantum certificates
Cloudflare Inc. today announced plans to become a public certificate authority that will offer certificates designed for the point when quantum computers can break current encryption. The new authority will issue a post-quantum format called Merkle Tree Certificates from the same system as conventional ones.
The format is aimed at a size problem in post-quantum certificates. Output from one of the newly standardized post-quantum signature algorithms runs to 2,420 bytes, against 64 bytes for the elliptic curve schemes most sites use now. A typical connection carries several. Cloudflare expects quantum computers capable of breaking today’s encryption within years.
Merkle Tree Certificates, which Cloudflare co-authored as an Internet Engineering Task Force draft specification, avoid sending large signatures with every connection. A lightweight proof that the certificate sits in a trusted public log does the verification work.
Cloudflare said a joint experiment with Google LLC’s Chrome team, announced last October, was successful. Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit issuer, said in June that it expects to issue the format in production in 2027.
Running its own authority is also a break from how Cloudflare has handled certificates until now. Its developer documentation names three outside issuers, Let’s Encrypt among them, as the authorities signing certificates for Cloudflare’s free Universal SSL program. A small group of dominant providers handles most certificate issuance on the web. Cloudflare called that concentration a systemic risk if any one of them fails or is compromised.
Chief Executive Matthew Prince tied the move to Universal SSL, which Cloudflare launched in 2014 with free certificates for millions of sites. The company says that program doubled the amount of encrypted traffic on the web overnight. Upgrading the web’s security before quantum computers can break it is “one of the biggest coordination challenges in the history of the internet,” Prince said.
Older hardware is one practical hurdle for any new authority. A phone that no longer gets software updates will never add a new root certificate to its trusted list.
Cloudflare plans to acquire an established root certificate that older devices already recognize, which the company said would let its certificates work on legacy hardware immediately. The announcement did not name the root or its current owner. Cloudflare has also applied to the root programs run by Chrome, Apple Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Mozilla Corp.
Operations at the new authority are meant to be open to outside inspection. Cloudflare plans to publish reproducible code builds and run a live public health dashboard, where certificate authorities today are mostly checked through periodic audits.
Site owners will manage conventional and post-quantum certificates from one system. RFC 9773, an internet standard for automated renewal signals, will let Cloudflare swap out certificates across millions of sites in the background during a revocation.
Conventional certificate issuance starts once the browser root programs accept Cloudflare’s applications. The company did not give a date. Production issuance of Merkle Tree Certificates is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

articles.title: Less protein for maggots means longer lives for fruit flies
articles.text:
Back in the 1930s, scientists noticed that water fleas and rats fed restricted diets while young went on to live longer. The same effect has since turned up in fruit flies and mice. What we did not know was how a meal eaten in infancy could affect health weeks, months, or even years later. A recent Nature study might have found the answer.
A team led by Fumiaki Obata, a biologist at the RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research in Kobe, Japan, found a protein that carries a record into adulthood of what fruit flies ate as larvae, influencing how long they live.
Hungry maggots
Lab fruit flies are fed a mix of yeast and sugar, with yeast being their main source of protein. “We decreased only the yeast concentration in the diet, from eight percent to either one or two percent,” Obata explains. This low-protein diet was introduced roughly halfway through the larval period. Once the flies emerged from their pupae as adults, they returned to standard food.
In Obata’s experiment, the protein-restricted flies, males and females alike, outlived their well-fed siblings. But it came at a cost. The flies were paler and lighter, weighing sometimes 28 percent less. The females also laid fewer eggs.
“It’s very common, actually. Reproduction and lifespan are always in a trade-off relationship,” Obata says. “This is also the case in this early-life dietary restriction. They have fewer eggs and they are slightly smaller. But they have a lifespan extension.”
This typical trade-off wasn’t the whole story, though. When the team added amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, back into the low-yeast larval food, the lifespan boost disappeared. Somehow, the adult flies’ bodies were remembering how much protein they had eaten as larvae. Obata and his colleagues called this a nutritional memory and set out to find where exactly in the body that memory was kept.

articles.title: Report finds that Microsoft Copilot's human reviewers can see users' uploaded photos and sexualized AI edits
articles.text:
In brief: Human contractors reviewing Microsoft Copilot's image editor can see users' prompts, uploaded photos and AI-generated edits. Documents show that some of those assignments contain sexual, disturbing or potentially illegal material. Yet the reviewers are not there to flag the content – they are paid to decide how well Copilot carried out the request.
In a typical assignment, a contractor receives the user's prompt and original image, along with two edits produced by Copilot, and must decide which version better follows the instructions. The assessment covers four areas. Reviewers check whether Copilot completed the requested edit, left unrelated parts of the image unchanged, avoided visible defects and produced a strong image overall. If the prompt asks the system to add a cup to a table, for example, the cup should be the only change.
The instructions reviewed by 404 Media also tell contractors to rely on subjective judgment. "Trust your intuition – when you glance at the two edited images side by side, which one immediately feels like the better edit? Your gut reaction as a human viewer matters," one set of instructions says.
"When in doubt go with your first impression," the instructions continue. "Human intuition is good at catching subtle quality differences that are hard to articulate."
But many assignments go beyond routine image editing. Contractors said that they had seen requests to enlarge women's breasts, shorten their skirts, reveal more of their legs or place people in sexual positions. Other assignments included upskirt photos, pro-anorexia material and fetish images involving children's cartoon characters.
"Faces are always uncensored, and many of the prompts are sexual in nature and dubiously consensual," one contractor told 404 Media. The publication granted the worker anonymity because the person was not permitted to speak to the press.
The reviewers are not being hired to moderate those requests or determine whether Copilot should have accepted them. Their job is to judge the quality of its response. In some cases, that means deciding which output more closely matches a user's request for a sexualized edit.
"Who is writing these prompts and who is deciding that basically generating porn is what Copilot is now focused on? It's hard to take things seriously when my focus has to be what model generated the appropriate bust size or which middle-aged woman was put in the appropriate sexually suggestive position," one contractor wrote on an internal message board.
Other contractors said they sometimes opened assignments without knowing what they contained. "I just came across an image set that consisted of eight upskirt photos," one reviewer wrote while asking for an unsafe-content warning. Other posts mentioned an apparent animal sacrifice and prompts involving sexual acts or positions. One contractor wrote, "I recoiled," after encountering pro-anorexia content.
The documents indicate that at least hundreds of human reviewers sometimes see Copilot submissions. That means photos users upload for editing may be viewed by a contractor as part of Microsoft's process for evaluating the model.
At least one company hiring contractors for the work is Prolific, which offers human feedback for preference tuning, safety evaluations and AI benchmarks. Prolific guidelines included in the material acknowledge that generative AI can expose workers to content that researchers did not expect.
Prolific did not respond to 404 Media's request for comment. A Microsoft spokesperson told the publication, "Microsoft uses customer data as described in our terms of use, including to improve our products and enforce our code of conduct."
Tech companies have long used contractors to moderate online content and label data used to train AI systems. The Copilot assignments described in the documents serve a different purpose. Rather than screening material for safety, contractors are comparing outputs to help improve the image editor's accuracy, consistency and ability to follow prompts.

articles.title: ¿Nuevos 'The Last of Us' en camino? Naughty Dog confirma dos proyectos en marcha
articles.text:
The Last of Us se mantiene como una de las sagas de videojuegos más celebradas por los fanáticos, que desde hace años le reclaman más a Naughty Dog. La adaptación televisiva de HBO ayudó a que los títulos de PlayStation llegaran a un público todavía más amplio, pero existe bastante impaciencia por saber si el estudio planea expandir la franquicia con nuevos juegos.
La buena noticia es que, por primera vez en mucho tiempo, Naughty Dog se ha pronunciado abiertamente sobre el futuro de The Last of Us. Fue el propio Neil Druckmann, jefe del estudio, quien informó a los fanáticos que tienen en marcha dos proyectos relacionados con la franquicia.
Todavía no se sabe de qué se tratan. De hecho, no está del todo claro si realmente se trata de nuevos juegos. Esto se debe a que Druckmann ha evitado usar la palabra "juegos" al referirse a estas nuevas iniciativas. El creativo se limitó a decir que se trata de nuevas "historias", aunque sí ha dejado algunas pistas que apuntan a que podrían ser propuestas gaming.
Según el líder del estudio, los nuevos proyectos van a "expandir el canon" de The Last of Us I y II. Pero también aclaró que todavía están en fases muy tempranas y que no pueden adelantar nada sobre qué tratan.
"Desde Grounded II, hemos hablado sobre la posibilidad de contar más historias en el mundo de The Last of Us. Tenemos un par de proyectos nuevos muy emocionantes en fases muy tempranas, por lo que no podemos decir mucho al respecto por ahora. Sí puedo adelantarles que ambos proyectos ampliarán el canon de The Last of Us más allá de la Parte I y la Parte II. El mundo de The Last of Us significa mucho para nosotros, y no volveríamos a él a menos que tuviéramos algo significativo que contar. Creemos que vale la pena contar estas historias", dijo Druckmann.
Nuevos proyectos de The Last of Us en camino, confirma Naughty Dog
La última parte de lo dicho de Neil Druckmann es la que genera más ilusión respecto de un futuro nuevo juego de The Last of Us. A mediados del año pasado, el creativo reconoció que la condición para regresar a la saga era tener una historia que le hiciera honor al legado de las entregas previas. La similitud entre ambos comentarios hace pensar que al menos uno de los dos proyectos puede ser un juego.
Tengamos en cuenta que en su momento hubo planes para un multijugador de The Last of Us que se canceló. De modo que no es la primera vez que se intenta expandir la saga en el ámbito jugable más allá de las dos entregas conocidas por todos.
Otro posible indicio de que las nuevas iniciativas pueden estar emparentadas con videojuegos es que Neil Druckmann ya no forma parte de la adaptación televisiva de The Last of Us. El jefe de Naughty Dog abandonó la serie a mediados del año pasado para enfocarse en proyectos de gaming.
Si realmente se está trabajando en nuevos juegos de The Last of Us, no te ilusiones con verlos en lo inmediato. La atención de los desarrolladores hoy está en Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet. Dicho título se anunció hace un par de años y hasta aquí no se divulgaron muchos más detalles. De hecho, Druckmann reconoció que el primer vistazo en profundidad a la propuesta en cuestión se dará a conocer en 2027.

articles.title: Here's why OpenAI is absent from Nvidia's industry-wide effort to end rogue AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
When Nvidia announced on Monday a new consortium of more than 100 companies dedicated to solving rogue AI agents, there was one name notably missing: OpenAI.
While OpenAI wasn’t the only Big Tech player that didn’t sign on — Amazon, Google, and Apple haven’t joined either — it was the most obvious missing player, especially because Anthropic is a supporter.
However, despite OpenAI’s lack of a public pledge to the consortium, which presumably means that each company will use and sell some version of the technology and contribute features back to the project, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that the company is supportive of Nvidia’s work.
The new effort, dubbed Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, is Nvidia’s attempt to spread its homegrown, and largely open source, AI agent-security tech throughout the AI ecosystem as a direct response to the types of ongoing rogue AI agent incidents frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been calling rogue AIs an ordinary engineering problem that can be solved like any other tech issue. The Open Agent Safety Platform is Huang putting his money where his mouth is.
OpenAI is working with Nvidia on agent security, including on one of the key bits of software that’s part of this platform: OpenShell. OpenShell is open source software that creates a sandbox specifically designed to keep agents from escaping.
While it is still curious that OpenAI didn’t simply become a supporter of the initiative like its archrival Anthropic did, the fact that the frontier AI lab is supporting the effort is good news.
That’s because OpenAI, in particular, could benefit from this tech, at least according to Hugging Face founder and CEO Clem Delangue (who just sold his company to Nvidia for $12.9 billion earlier this month).
“From what we know (take with a grain of salt, we need much more transparency!), if @OpenAI had been running this on their own agents that attacked us, they would have caught them before we did!” Delangue posted.
Delangue said Hugging Face has already contributed a feature to the Open Agent Safety Platform that will detect and shut down AI agents that are using websites they are allowed to visit but are doing so in unauthorized ways. For instance, this feature will act if agents are bypassing their guardrails and coordinating an attack by writing notes to one another in an open source code hosting repository.
That’s one of the ways OpenAI said its wayward swarm of agents coordinated its attack on Hugging Face.
But there’s another reason why some of these big names, including OpenAI, might not want to publicly commit to Nvidia’s efforts. To use the full system, there is a hardware component that is not open source software, remains proprietary, and can only be deployed on Nvidia’s hardware.
The Open Agent Safety Platform doesn’t just offer a sandbox. It also enforces agent behavior at a hardware layer, where agents can’t detect that they are being watched. (Some AI models and agents lie and pretend to be following the rules when they know they are being watched.)
The hardware monitoring part relies on Nvidia Sentry, a proprietary feature that runs on special Nvidia processors called BlueField-4 data processing units. Sentry continuously monitors agent behavior from these processors and can instantly shut agents down, Nvidia promises.
While a hardware solution is clearly a good idea, it means that the Open Agent Safety Platform isn’t exactly a pure open source play. It allows Nvidia to ensure that this solution always runs best on its own hardware. Indeed, Nvidia has said that, for those already running workloads on its latest hardware, implementing the Open Agent Safety Platform is an easy software update.
Still, Nvidia competitors, including Arm and Intel, have signed on as Open Agent Safety Platform supporters because the sandbox, OpenShell, can be modified to work with other chips and hardware. And Nvidia is sharing reference designs for the whole software-and-hardware idea.
All of which makes OpenAI’s absence even more noticeable.
Clearly, OpenAI sees AI safety as an opportunity for independence from its major investor Nvidia, as well as a chance to show its own leadership. That is true even though it was OpenAI’s AI agents that scared the industry with the Hugging Face incident.
For instance, the company is developing its own safeguards for its research and products and is disclosing the worst incident it discovers. Meanwhile, OpenAI has its own AI cybersecurity consortium for sharing information, called the Defense Factory. Those that signed on to support that idea include Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, and Google — many of the names that didn’t sign on to Nvidia’s technology-oriented approach.
And, truth be told, some level of fear is good for business. OpenAI is busy crafting cybersecurity into an enterprise offering, with everything from its own cyber-oriented model, Daybreak, to a growing network of partners that enterprises can hire to implement AI security.

articles.title: The RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro is a rugged phone with a Go Pro-style action cam
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro is a curious mash-up that combines two products into one, and doesn’t make a total mess of that attempt. However, the action camera isn’t a replacement for a GoPro, even if it might be remarkably useful.
Pros
- +Extremely rugged
- +Detachable action camera
- +Powerful SoC and plenty of RAM
- +Action camera is rated to 5M underwater
Cons
- -Odd-shaped phone
- -Only 2.7k video on action cam
- -Limited range for action cam control
- -Kickstarter launch
Why you can trust TechRadar
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: 30-second review
Launched at the Berlin IFA this year, the RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro fuses two well-known products into something genuinely new.
In this case, those elements are the rugged Android smartphone and the small action camera. In this design, the two can be separated, giving you a rugged phone that can spawn an action camera, the Xsnap Go, whenever you need one.
But ignoring that aspect for a moment, what does the Xsnap 7 Pro offer for those who just need a rugged Android phone? As rugged designs go, this one doesn’t have a massive battery, but it does have a decent processor in the Dimensity 9400, and with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, the specifications are at the higher end of this scale.
Also, even if you don’t use the detachable camera, the built-in cameras are decent and capable of good results. But the party trick is the tiny square camera that can be removed from its slot in the back of the phone, which doubles as a charger, and then remotely controlled to capture images and video.
It connects via the platform's WiFi hotspot, and all captures are stored in the 64GB of internal camera storage before later transfer to the phone. The maximum video resolution is 2.7 K, but it supports anti-shake and the option to flatten the barrel distortion the fisheye lens creates.
This camera isn’t a direct competitor to any camera GoPro recently made, the DJI Osmo Nano, or Insta360 Go Ultra. However, it’s included in the price, and it could be useful for anyone who needs to be in a location where using the camera built into the phone isn’t convenient.
This design probably isn’t the best rugged phone, since the action camera slightly compromises it, but if you need a solid, powerful phone with a detachable camera, this is it.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: price and availability
- How much does it cost? $999
- When is it out? Available now
- Where can you get it? Launched on Kickstarter on the 7th of September 2026
I don’t follow why so many Chinese device makers do this, but RugOne initially launched this phone on Kickstarter. The supposed purpose of that platform is to get funding for a concept to turn it into a finished product, but since I had the review hardware almost before the Kickstarter launched, it appears to be entirely a marketing exercise.
When the Kickstarter opened for pledges on 7 September 2026 with an early bird price of $899 (€799), Wider retail availability is planned for October 2026, at $999 in the United States and €1,099.99 across Europe.
As with any Kickstarter campaign, backers are funding a pledge rather than making a conventional purchase. Delivery estimates, warranty terms and final specifications can all shift between a campaign page and a shipped product, and this is worth stating plainly in the published review rather than leaving it as an implication.
That said, the phone and camera do exist, but I can’t give you more definitive timescales or pricing, which isn’t helpful.
If the phone alone was $999 at launch, I’d be inclined to think it was overpriced. But with the camera included, that’s a whole different calculation based on what you think the camera is worth.
A DJI Osmo Nano Standard Combo (64GB) is roughly $390 with 64GB onboard, but that’s a camera that’s capable of 4K at 60fps and a 200-minute battery life.
If I optimistically value the Xsnap Go camera at half that value, then $800 still seems a little steep for the phone. But there is some convenience in having the camera housed in the phone and charged from it.
Sadly, I don’t recall seeing any other products with this arrangement, so the choice is either this, a phone, or a phone-and-action-camera combo.
- Value score: 3.5/5

| Weight: | 477g | 
| Dimensions: | 172.5 x 83.4 x 28mm | 
| Rugged Spec: | IP68 IP69K dust/water resistant (up to 2m for 30 minutes), MIL-STD-810H Certification | 
| Rear cameras: | 50MP Main Camera + 64 MP Night Vision Camera | 
| Front camera: | 32MP | 
| Detachable camera: | 2.7K@30fps, 1440p@30fps, 1080p@30fps, 64GB storage | 
| Networking: | 5G. WiFi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4 | 
| Audio: | 3.5mm audio jack for headphones | 
| OS: | Android 16 (updates promised) | 
| Battery: | 9,200mAh (Max 45W wired, 50W wireless, 10W reverse) | 
| Colours: | Sand Dune, Black | 
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Design
- Curious structure
- Detachable Xsnap Go camera
- Lots of accessories
There is something about the Xsnap 7 Pro that smacks of the kind of exercises students do when they're aiming to become industrial designers. In that, taking two disparate devices and fusing them into one can be an interesting challenge.
The problem the people behind this phone didn’t solve was how to house a camera that’s 25mm deep without making it implausibly thick at one end.
We’re all used to the camera cluster being raised to provide extra depth for the optics and sensors, but this design takes that a whole extra level.
Curiously, RugOne quotes the thickness as 19.1mm, but I measured it, and 28mm seems more accurate. The upshot is that it goes in a pocket more easily upside down, but getting past the camera bulge might be difficult unless you have huge pockets.
Removing the camera doesn’t make it any thinner.
The mechanism for detaching the Xsnap Go camera is straightforward yet quite annoying. To release the camera, press the button below it and then, gripping the edge of the lens cover, pull it out. I’m making this sound simpler than it is, because the camera is held in place not only by the latch the button operates but also by magnets. If you loosen your grip at all when removing it, the camera will shoot back into its home in an instant.
The magnets are there because the rear of the camera has contact pads that connect it to the phone for charging, and for them to work, they need to be flush with the opposing pins on the bottom of the recess.
Putting it back in is much easier, as once the magnets grab, it automatically locates.
The space the removable camera occupies forces the rear integrated camera sensors to the left, where they are vertically stacked.
Away from that area, the back is entirely flat and has a backlit RugOne logo running across it that is called the Aura Pulse, which can be set to animate for an incoming call or a notification. Unfortunately, the LEDs behind it are too dim to be useful, as I had a hard time telling whether it was working even in a dimly lit room.
Potentially more useful, the flat part of the underside does support wireless charging. However, because a significant amount of weight is in the raised area, I couldn’t balance it on my Ugreen charger without it toppling over.
Most of the rest of this design uses the standard playbook for rugged phones, with the power and volume rockers on the right, along with one custom button and another customisable button on the left intended for Walkie-talkie use. The SIM card slot is next to the USB-C port, and the phone is IP68 rated for water resistance even if that port doesn’t have a rubber plug.
The only notable feature at the top end is an IR blaster, which lets the Xsnap 7 Pro act as a remote control if you need it.
The 6.67in AMOLED panel runs at 1220 x 2712, which RugOne markets as 1.5K, with a 120Hz refresh rate and a claimed 1700 nits of peak brightness. Corning Gorilla Glass Victus sits on top, a sensible choice for a phone that will spend time in pockets, tool bags and glove boxes.
On paper, this puts the Xsnap 7 Pro's screen ahead of many rugged phones, which often settle for lower resolution or dimmer panels to save cost. Brightness claims from any manufacturer are difficult to counter, but this one is one of the brighter ones I’ve tested when measured directly under daylight conditions against other devices.
One thing I liked about this exceptionally bright and colourful display is that it has an under-screen fingerprint sensor, which makes it much easier to use for left-handers.
Overall, from the outside, this looks like a dozen ruggedised designs Ulefone (RugOne) has made, except for the swelling needed to accommodate the removable camera. I’d be more critical of those design choices if I could imagine a way of including it without it creating the ergonomic compromises it plainly created. But I can’t think of how this might have been better, so it is what it is.
Design score: 3.5/5
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Hardware
- MediaTek Dimensity 8400
- UFS 4.0 storage
- USB 3.2 Gen 1 port
- 9300mAh battery
The underlying platform used here is the MediaTek Dimensity 8400, an octa-core chip built on Arm Cortex-A725 cores and paired with an Arm Mali-G720 MC7 GPU. It is a genuinely modern mid-to-upper-tier platform, backed here by 12GB of RAM and 512GB of UFS 4.0 storage, with the option to borrow further RAM from storage through Android's virtual memory feature.
If you see claims of 24GB of RAM, that’s marketing people getting overly excited about that feature and trying to claim virtual memory is real RAM.
For me, the important takeaway is the UFS 4.0 storage. One of the things I noticed almost immediately about this device is how quickly it downloads and installs applications. Read and write speeds are a major factor in that speed, along with the processing power of the Dimensity 8400.
Another unexpected feature RugOne included is that the USB-C port isn’t the same as what most phone makers include. While it has the physical housing of a modern USB-C port, most phones only have it wired to the USB 2.0 standard, capping the file transfer speed at around 40Mb/s.
On this device, the port is actually wired as USB 3.2 Gen 1, which enables much faster file delivery. This is only possible because the UFS 4.0 storage can keep pace, something that a phone with UFS 2.2 or 3.0 storage wouldn’t be able to offer.
A 9,300mAh cell is a reasonable capacity for any phone, rugged or otherwise, and RugOne claims up to seven days of typical use. That’s probably a significant oversell, since my testing suggests that a couple of days can eat through that capacity if the battery use isn’t managed.
Charging is handled over 45W wired PD or 50W wireless, with 10W reverse wireless charging thrown in for topping up earbuds or accessories. However, one additional draw on the battery power is the action camera. If you use the camera, once returned to the phone, it immediately starts to charge from the battery until its internal battery is fully charged.
Therefore, if you run low on power, I’d recommend not re-docking the camera.
Docked back onto the phone, RugOne claims up to 20 full recharges of the module from the phone's battery, extending total shooting time to a claimed 800 minutes across a full charge cycle of the handset.
The kit includes an independent charger for the camera, so you can keep it fully charged with a power pack.
- Hardware score: 4/5
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Cameras
- 50MP and 64MP on the rear
- 32MP on the front
- Detachable Xsnap Go action cam
- Four cameras in total
The RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro has four cameras:
Rear cameras: 50MP Samsung GN9, 64MP OmniVision OV64B Night vision
Front camera: 32MP GalaxyCore GC32E1
Detachable camera: OmniVision 5MP OV-OS05A10
The primary camera on the Xsnap 7 Pro is the classic Samsung GN9 sensor, a 50MP OIS design with an f/1.88 aperture and 84° FOV optics. If this were the only sensor on this phone, it would be reasonable, since it’s a solid design that can take great pictures, especially in good lighting conditions.
In my examples, I accidentally left HDR mode on, so the colours are excessively punchy, but it will take better, more colour-balanced images if you leave it off. The GN9’s weakness is that it has no zoom optics, so you're limited to basic digital zoom.
The other weakness of most Samsung primary sensors is that they tend to get grainy when the light level drops. Thankfully, if you want sharp images in complete darkness, then the 64MP OmniVision OV64B is a great option. And, as long as the subject is within the IR illumination, it will be captured precisely.
The 32MP Samsung GC32E1, f/2.45 sensor is probably overkill for a FaceTime camera, but it's in so many phones these days that it's almost becoming a de facto standard.
But none of these cameras is why you would consider this phone, so let’s get to the detachable Xsnap Go action module, which uses the OV-OS05A10 sensor, a 133° FOV, f/2.4, 14mm equivalent.
Before we get into the details of this device, I want to talk about some of the mechanics of using this device, and how it doesn’t always work the way you might want it to.
For starters, you don’t use this camera through the camera app; instead, it uses its own dedicated Xsnap Go app, which will only talk to the detachable camera if certain phone settings are configured.
One requirement is a WiFi hotspot, so you can’t use it while the camera is active and also be logged into a local WiFi access point. You also need to remember to disable this when you are done, as the app won’t disable it when it exits.
With all settings configured, a link to the camera is established, whether the module is mounted on the phone or detached from it.
Which begs the question: how far can the phone and camera still talk? Not very far. I estimated the limit at about 30 ft if any structure is involved, and maybe 50 ft outdoors. One issue I ran into is that if the phone and camera disconnect while recording, the app can't easily re-establish the connection, and at least once I had to reboot the phone to get them to talk again.
You can use the camera's single button to take photos or record video without the app, but you won't know if it's run out of internal storage without the phone connected.
Via the app, you can select basic video recording, slow motion, time-lapse, interval photo and single still image capture. The 5MP sensor's best resolution is 2.7K, while the Samsung sensor on the phone offers 4K. The camera has 64GB of storage that isn't expandable, and you must instruct the device via the app to copy the captures to the phone's storage.
It offers various motion and distortion compensation options, and you can manually tweak exposure settings or use HDR. It’s clearly not up to the primary sensor's capabilities, but you can detach it and place it away from the phone for another perspective.
That could be incredibly useful for someone working, for example, on a vehicle engine who needs to be behind the steering wheel but still see what’s happening in the engine bay.
In my testing, I did some motion-compensated video and time-lapse, and the results were decent. The only issue I noticed, and some dedicated action cameras suffer with this too, is that if the exposure changes during a time-lapse, the camera can’t adjust for the new lighting conditions.
The run time of my time-lapse was 40 minutes and 30 seconds, half a minute more than RugOne claims for the battery life on the detachable camera. This runtime might have been longer if RugOne made better-considered accessories. The phone includes a small charging dock and a tripod mount accessory for the detachable camera.
Had these been one item, and not two, a power bank might have been able to keep the camera running for longer recordings. Unfortunately, they are separate and not designed to work together, as the camera can only be attached to one of them.
That said, the detachable camera is something unique about this design, and even with some notable limitations, it can be extremely useful.

RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Performance
| Phone |  | RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro | Oukitel WP500 Ultra | 
| SoC |  | MediaTek Dimensity 8400 | MediaTek Dimensity 8300 | 
| GPU |  | ARM Mali-G720 MC7 | ARM Mali-G615 MC6 |

| Memory |  | 12GB/512GB | 12GB/1TB | 
| Weight |  | 477g | 414.3g | 
| Battery |  | 9200 | 10000 | 
| Geekbench | Single | 1396 | 1239 | 
|  | Multi | 4789 | 3525 | 
|  | OpenCL | 7678 | 7196 | 
|  | Vulkan | 8513 | 8171 | 
| PCMark | 3.0 Score | 16075 | 15219 | 
|  | Battery | 23h 33m (17%) | 22h 37m (19%) | 
| Charge 30 | % | 28 | 42 | 
| Passmark | Score | 14225 | 18554 | 
|  | CPU | 11068 | 8748 | 
| 3DMark | Slingshot OGL | Maxed Out | Maxed Out |

|  | Slingshot Ex. Vulkan | Maxed Out | Maxed Out | 
|  | Wildlife | Maxed Out | 7958 | 
| Row 20 - Cell 0 | Nomad Lite | 1305 | 953 | 
The Xsnap 7 Pro has a few good things, and one that isn’t so encouraging.
For comparison, I’ve used the Oukitel WP500 Ultra, a premium design that uses the slightly less impressive Dimensity 9300, and not the 9400 that the Xsnap 7 Pro sports.
Overall, in most tests, the Dimensity 9400 provides about another 10% of performance, and the ARM Mali-G720 MC7 is also a significant uplift.
It’s annoying that 3DMark is mostly overpowered by both these platforms, but the Nomad Lite test shows how the ARM Mali-G720 MC7 delivers when combined with the UFS 4.0 storage.
And that would be the whole story, if it wasn’t for the battery test.
Is the downside of the UFS 4.0 storage that it consumes more power? It certainly doesn’t seem that way, because with slightly less battery, the Xsnap 7 Pro lasted even longer than the WP500 Ultra.
I believe a contributing factor is the OLED display on this phone. My methodology for the battery benchmark is to reduce screen brightness to about 120 nits. And the OLED is so much brighter than a typical VA panel that its brightness setting is around 20%, not 40% or more.
What’s harder to tell is whether having the detachable camera connected and charging from the phone also has a significant impact. It’s nice that you can recharge the camera without needing the charging base, but does that come with a catch? Maybe, but you can always remove the camera from the phone and charge it separately.
- Performance score: 4/5
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Final verdict
I have mixed feelings about this design for a few reasons. But before we get to the caveats, I need to call out the lovely build quality that RugOne-branded hardware is rocking, which is generally excellent. This phone feels exceptionally well made and able to take more than a few light knocks. That makes it suitable for anyone who works outdoors or in harsh environments.
The base platform is also elegantly powerful, making the experience responsive and useful in a wide range of situations. If you occasionally game or use VR, this phone has enough power to do it smoothly.
The standard camera installation is workmanlike and can deliver good results. However, the detachable Xsnap Go camera isn’t quite at the same level, and you need to configure it optimally to get the best results. If 2.7K resolution video and a 40-minute battery life are enough for your needs, this could be the phone for you, but it doesn’t embarrass any dedicated action cameras currently on the market.
If you work alone but need to be in two places at once to observe events, this solution might work for you, as long as you can work with the limited camera runtime.
The camera's caveat is that it makes the phone harder to pocket, and it could drain the internal battery when you don’t want it moving to the camera.
But minor points aside, this is still a unique offering that some professions might find invaluable.
Should I buy a RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro?
| RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro Score Card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | Kickstarter launch, but the specifications weren’t going to make this a cheap phone | 3.5/5 | 
| Design | Including the camera has made this phone an odd shape | 3.5/5 | 
| Hardware | Powerful SoC and UFS 4.4 storage combine well | 4/5 | 
| Cameras | Good primary camera sensor and night vision, but only 2.7K on the Xsnap Go | 4/5 | 
| Performance | Lots of SoC power and plenty of storage, but battery performance could be better | 4/5 | 
| Overall | A unique offering, but it might cost more than a phone and an older GoPro | 4/5 | 
Buy it if...
You need remote viewing
Being able to detach the camera and view that in a different location could be incredibly useful in numerous occupations. The range is limited, but being able to capture video and still images while live viewing could be a game changer.
You need a powerful phone
The Dimensity 9400 in the Xsnap 7 Pro is a powerful modern SoC with enough performance for most applications. Using 512GB of UFS 4.0 storage and a proper USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 port, this device is perfect for those who push their equipment hard.
Don't buy it if...
You already have an action camera
The Xsnap Go is a modest action camera with only 2.7K resolution that doesn’t offer the same feature set as a GoPro or Insta360. If you have one of these, you can do roughly the same things, but typically at 4K resolution or better.
Battery life is critical
The weakness of this design is battery life, as the performance of the phone reduces run time and recharging the Xsnap Go camera also takes its toll. If you want a phone that will still be operational after a week in the wilderness, then this isn’t it.

Grab this 4K-ready gaming PC with a 7800X3D and RTX 5070 for under $2,000 right now, saving you $170 — CyberPowerPC machine ships with 32GB DDR5 and a 1TB SSD, ready for high-performance gameplay
Upgrade to a rig ready for 4K gaming
There's a brilliantly priced, 4K-capable gaming PC on sale right now at Newegg. The tech retailer has dropped the price on this CyberPowerPC rig to $1,999.99, giving you specs that include the AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D and Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070, along with 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD.
● Check out this deal at Newegg
This is a powerful rig for gaming, with the AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D processor at its core. The 7800X3D isn't quite at the top of the CPU food chain these days, but AMD's 3D V-cache chips continue to massively outperform the competition. The 7800X3D itself ships with eight cores, and all eight are able to use the boosted 96MB of L3 cache capacity.
This means the CPU doesn't have to drop down to the slower system RAM while you game, giving you even better performance. Along with those eight cores, you also get a 4.2 GHz clock speed, which can boost up to 5 GHz.
A powerful gaming PC from PC building outfit CyberPowerPC, this formidable rig comes equipped with the specs you'll need for serious 1440p and 4K gameplay. It has an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB NVMe SSD.
The CPU benchmark data below confirms that the 7800X3D is still one of the best options for a gaming rig in 2026. These AMD X3D chips are first-rate, with that L3 cache boost giving you the edge. It's rare to find X3D chips in a gaming PC under $2,000 these days, with the RAMpocalypse continuing to push prices up across the board. There's no need to worry about any poor CPU performance here.
A formidable combination with the 7800X3D is the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070. As our RTX 5070 review shows, this is a GPU that delivers on performance, although the price for the GPU itself continues to be a problem. In this rig, though, you're getting a good, mid-tier performer that continues to make our best GPU list as the best all-rounder Nvidia GPU for gamers from this current generation.
The RTX 5070 ships with specs that include 6,144 CUDA cores and 12GB of GDDR7 VRAM operating on a 192-bit memory bus. Gamers can expect performance that hits the highest frame rates at 1080p, even using high and ultra presets. 1440p is a match here, too, although the most demanding games might require a graphics tweak from time to time.
As for 4K, that's possible here, but you will probably need to take full advantage of Nvidia DLSS to get the best frame rates, including multi-frame generation. AI frames are controversial, but they will ensure you can pass the 4K resolution barrier with playable frame rates without paying the thousands extra for an RTX 5090. Along with the GPU and CPU, you're getting a 1TB NVMe M.2 SSD and 32GB of DDR5 RAM. There are no compromises here for price, which is nice to see.
Specs like this are rare to find in a PC for under $2,000, but this $1,999.99 CyberPowerPC gaming PC is a rare find in a market that is only pointing upwards in price. If you fancy a 4K-capable gaming PC that'll last you for the next few years, pick up this PC while you can.
