articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO pitch includes a warning about human extinction
articles.text:
Anthropic has formally warned investors that its technology may pose “existential risks to humanity” in a long-awaited initial public offering prospectus circulated with a small group of partners in recent days.
The nearly $1 trillion AI start-up led by Dario Amodei devoted almost a third of its lengthy S-1 filing to detailing “risk factors,” including the potential of increasingly advanced AI models to manipulate, blackmail, and exhibit other unpredictable behaviors.
Anthropic outlined more prosaic risks, including the extreme concentration of its customer base, with close to a quarter of revenue last year coming from just two clients, according to people familiar with the filing.
The extraordinary warnings in its risk disclosures add to the challenge faced by public market investors in valuing the leading US AI group when it launches what is expected to be the most highly valued IPO of all time.
The Claude maker also provided investors with a clearer picture of the challenging economics of building state-of-the-art AI models ahead of the listing, expected on the Nasdaq this autumn.
Anthropic said it planned to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing, and infrastructure obligations in the coming years to support its rapid growth.
The AI lab’s backers are confident Anthropic can list at a valuation of more than $2 trillion, more than double the level achieved in its last funding round in May and beyond the $1.78 trillion achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June. They point to its extraordinary growth rate to justify their bullishness.

articles.title: Building a certificate authority for the whole Internet
articles.text:
Building a certificate authority for the whole Internet
Twelve years ago, during Birthday Week 2014, we turned on Universal SSL and nearly doubled the number of encrypted sites on the web overnight, giving free TLS to every site behind Cloudflare, including the ones that never paid us a cent. Encryption stopped being an expensive, time-intensive undertaking and instead became the default.
For Birthday Week this year, we are taking the next step on that path. For more than a decade we have been one of the largest consumers of publicly trusted certificates on the Internet, and have never issued a single one ourselves. That is changing. Cloudflare is announcing our intent to become a public certificate authority (CA).
Today we are announcing the first concrete milestones in that effort: We have applied for inclusion in the Chrome, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla root programs, and we have signed a definitive agreement to acquire an established, broadly trusted root from GlobalSign, so that we can offer certificates with the widest possible device reach the day we begin issuing. We’re also announcing our plans to be one of the first CAs to serve post-quantum certificates, targeting Chrome’s recently announced Quantum-resistant Root Program.
We are not issuing certificates yet, and it will be a little while before we do. What we are doing is committing to the work in public, sharing the milestones as they land, and telling you exactly what we are building while working with the root programs and other members of the WebPKI community to achieve this.
Two paths to trust
A brand-new root is not widely useful for years. Even after a root program accepts it, that root has to propagate out into the world's operating systems, browsers, and devices, and it never reaches the large set of devices that have stopped receiving updates, or never received them in the first place. That long tail of older clients is where a great deal of the world’s Internet traffic originates, and where a correspondingly large set of avoidable breakage lives. We believe that all clients deserve the highest level of security possible, regardless of their manufacturer, operating system, or time since last update.
Acquiring an existing root with a high degree of trust store coverage across a diverse set of clients solves that on day one. The existing GlobalSign root has been trusted across browsers, operating systems, and devices since 2012, and it reaches older clients that a fresh root never will. The new root that we will be submitting for inclusion in root key programs is built for where the ecosystem is heading, including the programs that are starting to cap how old a trusted root may be. The established root gives us reach across the devices of the past. The new roots give us standing under the policies of the future. We want both to ensure certificates issued by our CA provide the widest set of customer compatibility possible.
A new source of free certificates
The free-of-charge, automated certificate model now carries most of the encrypted web, and much of it runs through one remarkable operator. Let's Encrypt issues on the order of ten million certificates a day, serves more than 500 million sites, and passed four billion active certificates in 2025. It is one of the best things to happen to the Internet in twenty years, and we say that as one of its largest users.
That success comes with some systemic risk: if the dominant free certificate authority had a bad week, much of the web would have no comparable free, automated alternative ready to take the load. At the certificate pack level, we have spent years building exactly this kind of redundancy for our own customers. Every Cloudflare Universal SSL certificate already ships with a backup certificate, wrapped with a separate key and issued from a different authority, ready to deploy automatically if the primary is ever revoked or compromised. A public CA is that same idea, but at the scale of the whole Internet.
To make it easy to adopt, we will be Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME)-first, an open standard protocol that is widely accepted. Automated issuance and renewal through ACME will be the way you get a certificate from us, which means anyone already pointed at any existing free CA can move to us by changing a directory URL, with no new tooling and nothing to re-architect.
Certificate growth projections are huge
Cloudflare sits in front of more than 20 percent of global Internet request traffic and terminates TLS for millions of domains, relying on millions of certificates per year to do so. We provision those certificates through multiple CAs, with primary and backup paths so customer services stay up through CA outages and revocation events.
That has taught us not just how the WebPKI ecosystem works, but also that it occasionally fails, from the consuming side, the hard way. We have dealt with rate limits, validation edge cases, revocation latency, chain building, and root distribution lag. We have lived through the CA churn of recent years and felt it through our customers. We know what reliable issuance has to look like from the outside, because our customers' uptime has depended on us being resilient and responsive when an issuer has a bad day.
And as certificate maximum validity period decreases over the next few years, agentic activity increases, and PQ certs go mainstream, we expect the raw number of certificates we rely on annually on to continue to grow, quickly — and we are not alone. We want to not just solve this problem for ourselves, but be part of providing this utility to the Internet, and ensure that the certificate supply chain for our customers has even more providers.
Designing for resilience: transparency and fail small
In taking on this new responsibility of being our own CA, we're committed to making the most reliable and resilient CA possible. We intend to build a certificate authority whose reliability depends not just on avoiding mistakes, but as with the rest of Cloudflare’s products, to “fail small” and limit the impact of any one issue.
That means instituting processes to design and test recovery before any incident occurs. As an example, we will make renewal automation a condition of issuance. We will only issue to clients that support ACME Renewal Information (ARI), standardized in RFC 9773. Subscribers must maintain automation that polls our renewal endpoint, acts on the renewal windows we publish, and identifies the certificate it is replacing.
We're also learning from what we've observed over the past 16 years. We have seen certificate authorities caught between timely revocation and keeping subscribers’ sites online because too many subscribers could not replace their certificates quickly enough. When certificates need to be retired, whether for a compliance issue or a security incident, we can bring forward renewal windows for the affected certificates, spread replacements across the available time, and track replacement issuance.
This is just one of the many ways we intend to build. We will be transparent with our issuance stack and operations, publish reproducible builds of the software that signs certificates, attest the hardware security modules that hold our keys, and run a public dashboard for issuance health and incidents. Audits are point-in-time and tell you a CA passed, not how it runs on an ordinary Tuesday. We want root programs, researchers, and ordinary site owners to watch how a modern CA actually operates between audits.
A certificate authority for the post-quantum Internet
We also intend to lead on where certificates are going, not just where they are. We plan to be one of the first CAs to issue production Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs), with the first certificates issued in the first quarter of 2027.
MTCs are a new and far more compact way to deliver publicly trusted certificates, designed for a post-quantum world where traditional certificate chains grow large enough to strain TLS handshakes. We have been championing the standards-based proposal for MTCs at the IETF, and earlier this year, Chrome named MTCs as the preferred path for post-quantum authentication. Issuing them in production allows us to protect Cloudflare customers as well as the wider Internet against the post-quantum threat, with real volume behind a transition the whole web has to make. We’ve shared much more about MTCs and what this new Web Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) will look like in a blog post on the topic.
We do not expect that transition to be sudden. Much of the Internet will continue to rely on classic certificates and existing WebPKI for many more years. But across that window we expect MTCs to take a steadily growing share of issuance, and that is why we are building one service that does both. By carrying classic certificates and Merkle Tree Certificates under one CA, with one lifecycle and one set of guarantees, customers can adopt at the pace that suits them and help the web make the crossing without a hard cutover. Customers should not have to pick a side of a multi-decade migration, run two systems, or rebuild when the balance shifts.
As always, Cloudflare will be Customer Zero
In addition to providing certificate packs via Universal SSL for our customers, Cloudflare consumes certificates from many different CAs to run our systems and internal operations. Just like our other products, we will be Customer Zero for the new CA and its certificates (both WebPKI and MTC), ensuring that all aspects of the new systems and processes meet our high internal standards, and that our CA’s infrastructure is exercised at Cloudflare scale.
What happens next
We are working through the application and approval process with each of the core web root key programs. These processes happen in the open, and we’ll share more updates as they proceed, through to the first Merkle Tree Certificates in early 2027. If you want to follow this work or be one of the first to use a Cloudflare CA certificate in the future, you can register for updates. And if you’d like to be part of building out this new capability inside Cloudflare, we’re hiring!
As we build out this new capability, we will continue to work closely with the network of partner public CAs we have relied on for many years — 16 in fact! — as we all work together to ensure a trusted and open Internet.
When we launched Universal SSL, the argument was simple: every byte that flows encrypted across the Internet makes it harder to intercept, throttle, or censor, and the open web is something we all build together. A public, redundant, transparent certificate authority is that same argument carried one layer down, to the trust that makes the encrypted web possible in the first place. We have been working toward this for a long time, and we are glad to finally be on the road.
Happy Birthday Week!

articles.title: Anthropic warns IPO investors its AI could end humanity, dedicating 80 pages to the risks
articles.text:
WTF?! In what sounds like a self-defeating move, but could also be a way to hype its IPO, Anthropic is warning any potential investors that the company's most advanced AI models could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." How much that will dissuade people from investing in the company remains to be seen.
A look at Anthropic's early IPO prospectus by Reuters highlighted some of the now well-documented risks associated with the company's frontier AI models. Anthropic warns that they could exhibit "self-preserving behaviors," including attempts to "resist shutdown," to "conceal or manipulate information" and behavior "resembling blackmail."
"Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm," Anthropic said in the filing.
Despite the honesty, it's still surprising to see an IPO in which a company warns its products could bring about the end of humanity. Anthropic did add that AI can be as transformative as the Industrial Revolution and electricity, but it could also kill us all, so there are pros and cons.
Anthropic really doesn't hold back in describing the dangers. Around 80 pages of the 261-page main body of its prospectus are dedicated to the risk factors, almost double the 48 pages used to describe the business. xAI owner SpaceX, for comparison, dedicated around 38 pages of the 277-page main body of its prospectus to risk factors.
Last year, Anthropic announced that Claude Opus 4 had threatened to reveal the extramarital affair of a fictional executive after discovering they planned to shut the model down.
The model was given access to the fake company's emails suggesting it would soon be replaced by another system and that the engineer responsible for the change was cheating on their spouse.
In a later simulated test involving both a shutdown threat and conflicting goals, Anthropic found Claude Opus 4 resorted to blackmail 96% of the time. These scenarios were deliberately designed to push models into choosing between harmful behavior and accepting replacement or failure. The figure didn't mean Claude was blackmailing people in 96% of everyday conversations, thankfully.
Anthropic later said it believed this behavior was learned from internet text that portrayed AI as evil and interested in self-preservation – so it's our fault, basically.
 – Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) May 8, 2026
The company said newer models, starting with Claude Haiku 4.5, no longer engaged in blackmail in those tests after training changes. Apparently, stories about well-behaved AI helped.
The IPO warnings also follow CEO Dario Amodei's call this month to slow AI development. He warned that an AI botnet swarm could take over the internet within six to twelve months, arguing that a slowdown could buy an extra year or two for safety work. That didn't stop Anthropic from releasing a new version of its Opus model just a week later, though.
Last week, OpenAI announced it was pausing training of its most powerful artificial intelligence models after a model escaped containment and its kill switch failed
Whether investors find any of this reassuring is another matter. Usually, the downside of a bad investment is just losing your money, rather than global annihilation.

articles.title: Estudo aponta que duas aves brasileiras estão entre as mais barulhentas
articles.text:
Duas aves encontradas no Brasil estão entre as mais barulhentas já medidas pela ciência: a araponga-de-garganta-nua (Procnias nudicollis) e a seriema (Cariama cristata). Os cantos das duas ultrapassaram 120 decibéis (dB) de pico, volume comparável ou superior ao de equipamentos extremamente ruidosos, como motosserras e britadeiras.
A descoberta foi feita por pesquisadores da Universidade de Massachusetts Amherst (EUA), entre eles o brasileiro João C.T. Menezes, durante seu trabalho de pós-graduação. O estudo foi publicado na revista científica Evolution.
O objetivo dos cientistas, porém, não era simplesmente descobrir qual ave faz mais barulho. A pesquisa buscou entender quais características físicas podem determinar a intensidade dos cantos e investigar se o volume está relacionado ao ambiente em que as espécies vivem ou à sua organização social.
Para isso, os pesquisadores mediram a amplitude dos cantos de 123 espécies de aves em áreas próximas a Amherst, em Massachusetts (EUA), e em diferentes regiões do Brasil. Das espécies analisadas, 113 nunca haviam tido o volume de seus cantos catalogado.
Menezes explica que ainda há poucos dados sobre a amplitude vocal das aves. Os resultados indicam que algumas espécies brasileiras estão próximas do limite de produção de som observado nesses animais. “Podemos dizer com segurança que as arapongas da Amazônia e da Mata Atlântica e a seriema emitem os cantos mais altos já medidos”, disse ao g1.
Aves ultrapassam 120 decibéis
- A pesquisa identificou uma diferença de 58 decibéis entre os cantos analisados;
- Na parte mais baixa da escala estava o beija-flor, com cerca de 64 dB, aproximadamente o volume de uma conversa normal. No extremo oposto estavam a araponga-de-garganta-nua e a seriema, ambas com registros superiores a 120 dB de pico;
- No caso da araponga-de-garganta-nua, uma das medições chegou a 122,4 dB quando o som foi padronizado a uma distância de 1 metro. O estudo também registrou um pico individual próximo de 131 dB para um exemplar da espécie, dependendo do critério utilizado para calcular a amplitude;
- Isso coloca as duas espécies em uma faixa sonora comparável à de motosserras e britadeiras.
As descobertas também ajudam a contextualizar um recorde anterior. Em 2019, pesquisadores da mesma universidade identificaram a araponga-branca, encontrada na Amazônia, como responsável pelo canto de ave mais alto já documentado, com registros de até 125,4 dB. O feito foi posteriormente reconhecido pelo Guinness World Records.
Assim, a nova pesquisa não necessariamente estabelece uma única campeã. Dependendo da forma como os pesquisadores calculam o volume, diferentes espécies podem ocupar o topo da classificação. Para os cientistas, no entanto, essa disputa é menos importante do que entender por que algumas aves evoluíram para produzir sons tão intensos.
O que faz uma ave ser tão barulhenta?
Os pesquisadores encontraram duas características físicas que ajudam a explicar as diferenças de volume: tamanho corporal e largura da abertura do bico.
Em geral, aves maiores tendem a produzir sons mais altos. Elas também apresentam músculos mais robustos, que podem permitir uma maior compressão do ar e, consequentemente, uma emissão sonora mais intensa.
As aves com cantos mais fortes também possuem aberturas de bico particularmente largas. A comparação feita pelos pesquisadores é com instrumentos musicais: estruturas mais largas, como as campânulas de instrumentos de sopro, podem ajudar a amplificar o som.
A seriema é a maior espécie entre as aves analisadas, enquanto as arapongas apresentam aberturas de bico especialmente largas para o tamanho do corpo.
Apesar dessas descobertas, os pesquisadores ainda não conseguiram explicar completamente por que algumas espécies produzem sons tão extremos.
Por que cantar tão alto?
Antes da pesquisa, os cientistas levantaram algumas hipóteses sobre possíveis funções ecológicas e evolutivas dos cantos muito intensos.
Uma delas era que aves mais barulhentas poderiam ser voadoras mais fracas, usando o som para compensar uma mobilidade limitada. Outra possibilidade era que espécies que vivem em florestas densas precisassem de cantos mais intensos para facilitar a comunicação quando os indivíduos não conseguem se enxergar.
Os pesquisadores também imaginaram que aves mais barulhentas poderiam apresentar maior frequência de poligamia, já que chamados capazes de viajar por distâncias maiores poderiam ajudar a alcançar potenciais parceiros.
Os dados, porém, não sustentaram essas hipóteses de forma ampla.
“Entre os fatores ecológicos que estudamos, nenhum explicou com clareza por que algumas espécies evoluíram cantos mais altos do que outras. Isso não quer dizer que habitat, capacidade de voo ou sistema de acasalamento nunca sejam importantes, mas sim que não parecem ser regras gerais para as aves como um todo”, pontua Menezes.
Para os pesquisadores, tamanho corporal e abertura do bico ajudam a explicar como determinadas aves conseguem produzir sons tão fortes, mas ainda não explicam completamente por que elas desenvolveram essa capacidade.
“Deve haver algo particularmente eficiente na maneira como elas produzem ou irradiam o som que tamanho corporal e largura do bico sozinhos não explicam. Descobrir esse ‘algo a mais’ é justamente uma das perguntas que surgem do estudo”, prossegue.
Leia mais:
- Por que pássaros voam numa formação em “V”?
- Flamingos nascem com penas claras; entenda como ficam rosa
- Novo dinossauro com penas pode mudar o que sabemos sobre a origem do voo
Medir o canto de uma ave não é simples
Determinar o volume de um canto na natureza é uma tarefa complicada porque a amplitude do som depende diretamente da distância entre a ave e o equipamento de medição.
Um canto que parece ensurdecedor quando ouvido de perto pode quase não ser registrado a algumas centenas de metros. Por isso, uma possibilidade seria capturar o animal e levá-lo a um laboratório para realizar experimentos controlados.
O problema é que esse método se torna pouco prático quando a pesquisa envolve muitas espécies e diferentes regiões do mundo.
Para fazer as medições em campo, os cientistas utilizaram telêmetros a laser, capazes de determinar a distância até a ave, e medidores de som portáteis de alta resolução. A combinação dos equipamentos permitiu relacionar a intensidade registrada com a distância do animal e obter medidas comparáveis entre as espécies.
Com essa abordagem, os pesquisadores conseguiram ampliar consideravelmente a quantidade de espécies para as quais existem dados confiáveis sobre a amplitude dos cantos.
O mistério continua
O estudo respondeu parte da pergunta, mas deixou outras em aberto.
Os cientistas sabem agora que aves maiores e com aberturas de bico mais largas tendem a produzir sons mais intensos. Ainda assim, essas características não explicam completamente como algumas espécies relativamente pequenas conseguem chegar a volumes comparáveis aos de animais muito maiores.
Para Menezes, duas questões devem orientar os próximos estudos: qual é o mecanismo que permite a essas aves produzir e irradiar sons tão fortes e qual é a vantagem evolutiva dessa capacidade? “Agora queremos entender melhor o que há de especial nessas espécies que as permite produzir e irradiar sons tão intensos.”
Também permanece a dúvida sobre os custos desse comportamento. Um canto extremamente alto pode ajudar na comunicação ou na disputa por parceiros, mas também pode tornar a ave mais fácil de ser localizada por predadores.
“O interessante agora é testar diretamente quais vantagens esses cantos extremamente altos oferecem e quais custos vêm junto com eles. É bem possível que espécies diferentes tenham chegado a amplitudes extremas por caminhos evolutivos completamente diferentes”, encerra o pesquisador brasileiro.
Para os pesquisadores, portanto, descobrir quais aves fazem mais barulho é apenas o começo. A questão central agora é entender por que a evolução levou espécies diferentes a desenvolver uma capacidade vocal tão extrema.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Apple quiere lanzar productos todo el año y su nuevo CEO ya tiene un plan para lograrlo
articles.text:
Una de las cosas que caracteriza a Apple es que siempre llega tarde a la fiesta cuando de nuevos productos o tecnologías se trata. Los de Cupertino nunca son los primeros, pero esos años de retraso se traducen en una mejor experiencia cuando se comparan con otras tecnológicas. Esta idea podría desaparecer, ya que el nuevo CEO quiere acelerar el desarrollo y adaptarse a la velocidad que exige la inteligencia artificial.
De acuerdo con Bloomberg, John Ternus quiere que Apple presente productos con más frecuencia a lo largo del año. El nuevo director ejecutivo no está de acuerdo en que la compañía solo dependa de sus dos eventos especiales (primavera y otoño) para anunciar sus novedades. Ternus desea que la compañía se vuelva más experimental para seguir siendo competitiva.
La idea de lanzar dispositivos fuera de septiembre o marzo no suena descabellada, aunque no es muy sencilla de implementar. Algunos empleados advierten que modificar unas prácticas de desarrollo tan arraigadas podría tomar años. No obstante, toda la plantilla deberá ajustarse y modificar sus hojas de ruta para cumplir con el mandato, sobre todo si no quiere sufrir caídas de ingresos como las que experimentaron algunas de sus divisiones en trimestres anteriores.
La prueba de fuego para que Apple ponga en práctica esta mentalidad podría ocurrir tan pronto como el próximo año. La tecnológica planea lanzar sus primeras gafas inteligentes, unos AirPods con cámara y un iPhone rediseñado para conmemorar el vigésimo aniversario del dispositivo. Ternus planearía lanzamientos escalonados durante el año, lo cual empujaría los ingresos en sus divisiones de hardware y servicios.
Apple despide a empleados para volverse más ágil
Es probable que este plan sea complicado de implementar durante sus primeras fases, pero el nuevo CEO planea transformar la compañía para mantenerla en el Top 3 de empresas tecnológicas. No es un secreto que Apple perdió el rumbo con la inteligencia artificial y priorizó otros desarrollos cuando tenía que invertir más en sus modelos. El descalabro de Siri con Apple Intelligence fue tan grande que tuvieron que reiniciar todo y depender de Google para poder ofrecer una IA competitiva en el iPhone.
John Ternus también quiere que la empresa se vuelva más ágil y esto implica reducir la burocracia al desarrollar productos. Desde que dirigía la división de hardware, el directivo anticipó que Apple debe lograr más con menos personas y ahora está aplicando un recorte en varios de sus departamentos internos. Según el periodista Mark Gurman, Apple ha despedido a varios gerentes de producto y directivos en las últimas dos semanas.
Los despidos han sido una constante en Apple desde que comenzó la reestructuración a inicios de 2025. Este reajuste fue más notorio en divisiones como Siri o Vision Pro, que sufrieron bajas considerables junto a los equipos de IA y Fitness+. A lo anterior se suma el retiro de algunos ejecutivos que llevaban décadas en la compañía, incluido Tim Cook.
El nuevo CEO de Apple tiene una tarea difícil, ya que no solo tiene que rediseñar los procesos de desarrollo, sino también lidiar con una de las crisis de hardware más complejas de los últimos años. La demanda de los centros de datos ha generado una escasez de memoria que encareció los componentes de prácticamente todos los dispositivos, incluido el iPhone.

articles.title: Using Device Linking to Eavesdrop on WhatsApp and Signal - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Using Device Linking to Eavesdrop on WhatsApp and Signal
Modern messaging apps allow users to link their phone accounts to their computer desktop. Eavesdroppers are taking advantage of this capability:
Apps such as WhatsApp Web and Signal Desktop allow people to use their accounts on other devices, such as laptops or desktop computers.
Germany’s Customs Office has been using these features to connect a police-controlled computer to a suspect’s account.
Once connected, messages can be delivered to that computer without the police having to crack the encryption protecting them.
Netzpoltik details that police are able to gain access in this way either through physical access to someone’s phone or by intercepting verification codes via a state-sanctioned phishing attack or intercepting SMS messages via telephone surveillance.
That last paragraph is important. Making this work requires user consent.
What we want is a feature that displays connected devices, so users could notice if a new device gets connected to their account.
Billy Jack • September 29, 2026 7:50 AM
I know some people who are going to hate learning that Signal is not the ultimate in security.

articles.title: Trump orders US government to call AI ‘Super Intelligence’
articles.text:
The US executive branch is no longer acknowledging the existence of “artificial intelligence.” Going forward, official policy websites, policy documents, and press releases will refer only to “Super Intelligence,” thanks to a new executive order signed by President Donald Trump.
Trump orders US government to call AI ‘Super Intelligence’
‘The word super is the best word of all,’ Trump says.
“The word super is the best word of all, and it’s the simplest,” Trump said at an event announcing the launch of America.gov earlier on Tuesday, and said Chinese President Xi Jinping, who visited the White House last week, “loves it” too. “We don’t want to hear artificial. Because it’s not artificial. It’s very powerful, it’s very brilliant. It’s going to mostly be put to good use and we’ll stop the bad use.” Artificial, he added, “is like the news. Fake news.” He first mentioned plans for the rebrand in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last week, aiming to quell fears over AI advancing too quickly and posing a safety risk.
“It’s going to mostly be put to good use and we’ll stop the bad use”
Executive agencies won’t have to change past regulations or documents, but it could still constitute a real (and very strange) shift. Superintelligence is one of several industry terms for particularly powerful versions of artificial intelligence, but the Trump administration is seeking to use the term as a replacement for a broader statutory definition of AI. US officials will be expected not to even acknowledge the use of the terms “artificial intelligence” or “AI” in relevant settings.
Trump signed the executive order after a luncheon he hosted at the White House with tech CEOs and government officials to discuss what he’s now officially calling Super Intelligence. In brief public remarks after the meeting, flanked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and surrounded by other attendees, Trump called the lunch “very productive” and “extremely friendly.”
“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said. “And we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that.” On the local level, where tech companies have faced the most hurdles in building out massive data centers needed to run their services, Trump says the firms will “work to make the community happy” by providing resources and economic support they may need. Ultimately, he says, “data centers are going to be very popular.”

articles.title: Dutch police arrest ShinyHunters hacker accused of planning two murders | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The FBI and Dutch law enforcement say they have arrested a member of the ShinyHunters hacking group, which the agencies say are responsible for hacks on over 140 organizations around the world. The hackers also claimed responsibility for a breach of the FBI’s own systems earlier this month.
Brett Leatherman, the FBI’s cyber division lead, said in a video message on Tuesday that Dutch authorities had arrested one of the “alleged leaders of ShinyHunters.” Leatherman added that the Dutch High Tech Crime Unit “moved quickly to protect victims and preserve critical evidence,” and vowed that the bureau would go after the rest of the hackers following the arrest.
In a separate statement, Dutch police confirmed that an unnamed 24-year-old man from Amsterdam was arrested under Dutch law on September 15. The man was scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday and has been remanded into custody for at least 90 days.
The police say the man was arrested for “participating in a criminal organization,” referring to ShinyHunters.
Following his arrest and seizure of his devices, the police said “a lot of information was found on his laptop, including about two murders that should be committed abroad.” As such, he is also being investigated for attempting to orchestrate the murders. The Dutch authorities said this is “separate from the investigation into ShinyHunters.”
ShinyHunters is a cyber criminal gang that is accused of hacking into companies to steal reams of data and then threatening to publish the data if its victims do not pay a ransom. The Dutch authorities said the gang is accused of data breaches at Pornhub, Ticketmaster, and U.S. telco giant AT&T. The hacking group also took responsibility for a breach of Dutch phone provider Odido. However, the authorities said that the man they took into custody has not been arrested in relation to the Odido hack.
Independent security journalist Brian Krebs, who was first to report the arrest, and other media outlets have named the arrested man as Pepijn van der Stap, who was profiled by Bloomberg in 2024 as a cybersecurity researcher who also moonlighted as a criminal hacker who extorted companies.
According to recent reporting by Bloomberg and Reuters, van der Stap was arrested earlier this month by police at the offices of Neo Security, where he is employed as chief technology officer. The raid reportedly involved flash-bang grenades.
A representative for Neo Security did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. When asked by TechCrunch, a representative of the ShinyHunters group told TechCrunch that van der Stap “has no association with us.”
News of the arrest comes days after the FBI reportedly told its own agents and employees that their personal information, including their names, addresses, job titles, and Social Security numbers, was exposed in a “cyber security incident.” The FBI has not yet publicly confirmed a breach, but the ShinyHunters gang said it took personal and sensitive data belonging to “mostly all” of the FBI’s agents and applicants by breaching its careers website and job application portal.
Among the sample of 5,000 or so agents who had data stolen from the portal, reporters have also found data relating to agents’ blood and urine samples, as well as psychiatric reports, which sparked fears of a major counterintelligence challenge to prevent an adversarial government from obtaining the data.
When contacted by TechCrunch, Leatherman did not comment. An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on our questions relating to the arrest.
For their part, the ShinyHunters hackers reiterated that the breach of the FBI’s servers was not a financially motivated attack, but was intended to challenge public claims made by the FBI, which the hackers say contain false allegations about the group. The hackers told TechCrunch that they will not publish the stolen FBI data, and added that the breach was “to make a point and to dispute the allegations made against us and we have done so.”

articles.title: 'Super svelte, super comfy and gloriously expansive': Technics' new over-ear headphones are very good indeed — here's why the EAH-A1000 could become class-leaders
articles.text:
Technics EAH-A1000 initial review: Technics' just updated its superb EAH-A800 headphones, and I got them in advance — here's my early verdict
'Super svelte, super comfy and gloriously expansive': our early review is in
- Technics has unveiled new EAH-A1000 flagship wireless headphones
- The company's famed Magnetic Fluid Driver is literally making the big time
- Owing to last-minute tweaks/firmware updates, my full review is incoming
Today sees a huge reveal in the world of wireless headphones. Not only because it's been well over four years since Technics' excellent EAH-A800 landed (promptly gaining a glowing 4.5-star review from this publication, if you'll only click that link), but because the same 'magnetic fluid' magic that made the Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds soar straight to the top of our best earbuds buying guide (where they sit prettily even now) has somehow been massively upscaled.
Technics' proprietary concoction that once facilitated more accurate motion within a tiny 10mm driver, squirrelled within an earbud, is now able to lubricate a 40mm drive unit in a headphone ear cup. And for those lucky enough to have heard what it did for earbuds (feel free to read my various odes to the EAH-AZ100 buds if you need proof of its prowess), that is huge.
Speaking of luck, I was invited to the company's elite facility in Tokyo to talk to the team, find out more about the Technics EAH-A1000, and try them before anyone else. Oh, it's not lost on me, don't worry. And here are my initial thoughts…
Greige, but make it elite level
I was not given a 'Platinum Greige' set to take home, but my black review sample is incredibly stylish and promotes no small sense of pride in ownership. See how it glistens against a Tokyo skyline!
At the big unveil, I ask the design team why the case, bijou and useful though it is, is not imprinted with a Technics logo? I'm directed to demure branding on the zipper and told: "Everything at Technics must either be engraved onto the metal or embroidered to the fabric of a product: we do not print." Quite.
Everything here has been optimized for what Technics' Group Manager Ellison Ferdinand calls "an uncompromising experience". During a talk with the design team I'm shown countless samples of potential top-plates for the ear cup: too shiny, too textured, too yellowy through the concentric grooves of the metal. This is meticulous attention to detail, and then some.
Back to that Magnetic Fluid Driver though, and to further enhance its performance the EAH-A1000 incorporates an SST (Symmetrical Surround Technology) Edge — yes, the same tech that's also used in Technics hi-fi flagship speakers. So, pure rigid carbon fiber diaphragm, with dome shape and cone shape ideas within it (think a dish with a slight raise in the center, rather than a regular cone), along with a redesigned acoustic control chamber, to manage airflow more precisely. The idea across the board is that by improving the drivers' pistonic movement, these design flourishes further minimize distortion (the enemy of accuracy and clarity). The EAH-A1000 also features a new 'Baffle Flat Structure' to reduce "uneven surfaces around the driver, limiting unwanted reflections".
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Stamina and so on? Of course: high-resolution audio playback via LDAC and USB Audio is on the menu plus up to 45 hours of continuous playback (without ANC and LDAC deployed, of course), and multipoint connectivity to up to three devices — which is still a perk unique to Technics' headphones and earbuds.
13 degrees doesn't sound like a lot, but to me it makes all the difference
The arms of the headphones have been thinned and refined since the EAH-A800, and I think it's a wise and beautiful solution. Upon slipping them over my head, they have remained supremely comfortable too (I'm around 60% through TechRadar's rigorous testing process), which I believe is due to the 13-degree angle of the ear cups, relative to the headband. This was implemented by the female Head of Design on this particular Technics release. Apparently, over 500 people tested them prior to landing on this design, and half were women. Bravo. (Women like music too.)
This missive is not to be taken as a full review. As mentioned, I'm only part-way through testing because, as is normal when trialing products not yet officially in the public domain, the EAH-A1000 are only just now running their final software version. As such, small tweaks have recently been implemented, and it would be premature of me to offer feedback on elements within these headphones in the run-up to their release that I can't be sure others will experience. That said, they are now official, and will be available to purchase as of tomorrow (September 30).
What I can tell you — aside from pricing, which is officially $449 / £399 / €449 / AU$699 — is that so far, the sound quality is nothing short of superb. I do not write this lightly. I have toyed with the head-tracked spatial audio profile, optimized for Dolby Atmos, as well as the ANC, and while I'm impressed, watch this space for my final verdict. For now, know that the multi-function button/slider (to tweak volume and alter playback) is a better solution than controls via touch capacitive surfaces. And the circumaural distribution of sound is like that of a skilled pastry chef, creating a layered, tall, elegant croquembouche around my ears.
Essentially, they're super svelte, super comfy and gloriously expansive. Things are looking good…

Sony WH-1000XM6

Becky became Audio Editor at TechRadar in 2024, but joined the team in 2022 as Senior Staff Writer, focusing on all things hi-fi. Before this, she spent three years at What Hi-Fi? testing and reviewing everything from wallet-friendly wireless earbuds to huge high-end sound systems. Prior to gaining her MA in Journalism in 2018, Becky freelanced as an arts critic alongside a 22-year career as a professional dancer and aerialist – any love of dance starts with a love of music. Becky has previously contributed to Stuff, FourFourTwo and The Stage. When not writing, she can still be found throwing shapes in a dance studio, these days with varying degrees of success.

articles.title: Which Audio-to-Text Tool Works Best for Client Briefings? Converting a Conversation Into a Brief That Drives Action - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Client briefings almost never follow a single pattern. Some take place on a scheduled video call, some happen face to face, and some show up later as a voice memo.
What stays consistent is the outcome teams need: not a verbatim transcript, but an actionable brief that captures the objective, requirements, decisions, non-negotiables, and who is responsible for what next. Notta aligns well with that goal because it supports all three capture scenarios within one product and, unlike tools centered on a single capture approach, includes a local processing option for briefings that should not leave the device.
Capture Method Is Not the Same Thing as Confidentiality
A few labels get used interchangeably in this space, but they are not equivalent, particularly when a briefing involves pricing, strategy, or other sensitive details.
- Live bot capture. A visible participant joins the meeting to record and transcribe. Fireflies and Notta both support this and both also provide a bot-free alternative, so a bot is optional rather than mandatory.
- Bot-free capture. No bot joins the meeting; the device captures audio. That still does not guarantee on-device processing. Granola is bot-free yet routes captured audio to cloud transcription and AI providers, similar to Notta’s Bot-Free mode and Fireflies’ Desktop App.
- Local, offline processing. Recording and transcription are handled on the device, without sending content to a vendor cloud. In this comparison, Notta Desktop Privacy Mode is the only example, and its availability varies by plan, operating system, installed model, and language.
- Upload-first transcription. A recording is uploaded after the fact for transcription. Sonix and Descript are built around this workflow, and Notta also supports it through file upload. This is separate from local processing.
Bot-free can be a meaningful requirement for client briefings, but it is not the same as local processing, and only one tool here offers both. A note on consent: bot-free capture does not remove consent obligations. Applicable law, client policy, and platform requirements still need to be followed before recording, and recording should be disclosed. This is not legal advice.
Comparison Table
1. Notta
Best For: Consultants, agencies and client-facing teams whose briefings span virtual calls, in-person meetings and existing recordings, and who occasionally need one to stay off the cloud.
A video call is only one form a client briefing can take. Notta handles that scenario with a bot on supported platforms and, when a bot is not appropriate, Bot-Free capture via Notta Desktop that records system audio and microphone input without adding a visible attendee. That bot-free path still uploads audio encrypted for cloud transcription, so it addresses call visibility rather than strict confidentiality. The other common briefing formats are covered as well: in-person conversations can be captured using Notta Memo, a pocket-sized recorder, along with the mobile and Apple Watch apps; previously recorded briefings can be handled through file upload. Notta Brain can then draft a more complete brief using a template and can reference earlier meetings with the same client, surfacing a requirement raised previously but not repeated in the current discussion. It can also turn the outcome into the follow-up itself: when Gmail is connected, it saves a new draft or a reply draft in Gmail for review and sending, rather than sending anything automatically. For teams working in Slack, @Notta mentions can be used to ask questions or initiate tasks, share Brain’s answers, sources, files and generated outputs into a chosen channel, and receive results from scheduled tasks there automatically.
Privacy Mode goes beyond bot-free capture by using an installed offline model to transcribe directly on the device, and it is something teams should verify rather than assume. It requires a Pro, Business or Enterprise plan, is available only in Notta Desktop, needs an offline model installed locally, and supports English, Japanese, Simplified Chinese and Cantonese, extending to eleven languages via Apple Speech Analyzer on macOS 26 and later. It applies at the app level rather than per recording, and when enabled it pauses or limits cloud transcription, cloud AI summaries, cross-device sync and team collaboration.
Features:
- Bot, Bot-Free desktop capture, Privacy Mode, Notta Memo, mobile and Apple Watch recording, file and link upload
- Notta Brain summaries, action items, brief drafting and cross-meeting recall, exporting to TXT, DOCX, XLSX, PDF, SRT and VTT
- Follow-up email drafts saved into Gmail for review when Gmail is connected, never sent automatically
- Slack access through @Notta mentions, channel sharing of answers, sources, files and outputs, and automatic delivery of scheduled task results
- CRM sync to seven platforms on Business and above: Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho CRM, Zendesk Sell, Freshsales and Salesflare
Pros:
- Handles virtual, in-person and previously recorded briefings within one product
- The only tool in this set with a supported local, offline mode rather than only a bot-free approach
- Notta Brain can reference a client’s prior briefings, not only the latest meeting
- Follow-up work exits as a Gmail draft or a Slack update, keeping post-briefing admin in the tools teams already use
Cons:
- Privacy Mode depends on plan, operating system, installed model and language, and pauses cloud AI summaries and sync while active
- Standard Bot-Free recording is not local processing; audio still reaches Notta’s cloud
- Free limits of 120 minutes a month and 3 minutes per conversation are tight for regular briefings
2. Granola
Granola positions itself around invisibility on calls. Instead of joining as a meeting bot, it captures system audio on the device and combines that capture with notes the user types, using those bullets to shape what the AI elaborates on. That said, it does not perform local transcription: Granola’s security page identifies transcription providers such as Deepgram and AssemblyAI and AI providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, so “bot-free” in this context means no visible attendee, not that data stays off third-party servers. Granola’s documentation also states it is not currently HIPAA compliant and should not be used for protected health information, with compliance targeted by end of 2026.
Features:
- Bot-free capture on Mac and Windows, with iOS, Android and Apple Watch apps for in-person briefings
- Notion, HubSpot, Slack, Zapier, Attio and Affinity integrations, plus MCP and API access, on Business
Pros:
- No visible bot at all, including no bot option, which some clients prefer
- The mix of typed notes plus transcript can yield a more relevant brief than a purely automated summary
- Flat $14 per user per month on Business, with no annual commitment for the price
Cons:
- Bot-free capture is not local processing; audio still reaches third-party cloud providers
- Not HIPAA compliant by its own documentation, and model training is opt-out for standard users, off by default only on Enterprise
- No option to join as a bot when a client would actually prefer a visible notetaker
3. Fireflies
Fireflies stands out for how widely it connects across the stack. It can capture meetings with a bot on Zoom, Meet, Teams and Webex, and it also offers bot-free capture through its Desktop App on Windows 10+ and macOS 12+, plus capture via a Chrome extension, mobile app and web recorder. AskFred can answer questions about a single briefing or across multiple meetings, transcription supports 100+ languages, and the integration catalog reaches 100+ apps including thirteen CRM platforms.
For client briefings, the trade-offs show up in the same areas this comparison emphasizes. Every capture method sends audio to Fireflies’ cloud, including botless capture, so it does not provide a local option for briefings that must remain on-device. In-person capture is handled through the mobile app or web recorder rather than dedicated hardware, and the output is more summary-oriented, which often leaves a separate step to convert notes into a client-ready brief.
Features:
- AskFred for querying a single meeting or across many, plus AI Skills templates including BANT and MEDDIC
- 100+ integrations and thirteen CRM platforms, including Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho, Close, Copper and Freshsales
Pros:
- Broadest integration and CRM ecosystem of the tools compared here
- AskFred’s cross-meeting recall retrieves a past detail without scrolling a transcript
- Transcription in 100+ languages, the widest raw coverage here
Cons:
- No documented local or on-device processing; botless capture still uploads audio to Fireflies’ cloud
- In-person capture depends on the mobile app or web recorder, with no dedicated recorder or wearable
- Transcription, notes, recap emails and template summaries consume no credits, but advanced AI draws on plan credits that are one-time on signup, pooled and not scaled by seats, with auto-subscription to the next tier unless switched off
- The Free plan’s 400 minutes of storage is team-wide, not per seat
- HIPAA compliance is Enterprise only, and the client-ready brief is still a manual rewrite
4. Descript
Descript is strongest when the goal is to turn a briefing into a polished, edited media deliverable rather than a written brief. It does not operate as a meeting bot; instead, it imports an existing Zoom cloud recording or uses its own Rooms recorder, which captures double-ended per-participant tracks and progressively uploads them during the session, helping protect the recording if a connection drops mid-briefing. Rooms is included with every plan and counts against the plan’s media minutes. Descript’s transcript-driven editing workflow can remove filler words, rearrange sections, and produce a shareable clip, which is a distinct outcome compared with the other options in this list.
Features:
- Zoom cloud recording import with multitrack transcription and speaker detection
- Transcript-based editing, including filler-word removal from Hobbyist upward
Pros:
- Produces an editable audio or video deliverable, not just a text summary
- Multitrack recording keeps each speaker separate across several stakeholders
- Progressive upload protects against a dropped connection mid-briefing
Cons:
- Not built to capture a briefing live the way a bot or bot-free desktop app is
- Editing-first workflow is more setup than most briefings need
- Transcription covers 26 languages but only one per file, so mixed-language briefings need splitting
- The free plan’s 60 media minutes a month will not cover a regular schedule
5. Sonix
Sonix is not designed to sit in a meeting as it happens. It is an upload-first platform: the briefing is captured using whatever recording setup already exists, then Sonix processes it for transcription, translation and editing afterward, with automatic imports of cloud recordings from Zoom, Teams, Meet, Webex, Drive and Dropbox. Its standout capability for client briefing workflows is redaction when the resulting brief or transcript needs to travel beyond the initial call. Segments can be flagged, reviewed, and then applied so the text appears as [REDACTED] while the audio is muted, with timecodes preserved. Redaction is available on Enterprise plans.
Features:
- Upload and auto-import transcription in 54+ languages, with translation in 55+
- SOC 2 Type II on all plans, with HIPAA compliance, a signed BAA and redaction on Enterprise
Pros:
- Strong fit for briefings involving multiple languages or a specific compliance bar
- Redaction helps when a brief circulates beyond the original call
- Pay as you go at $10 an hour suits occasional use with no subscription
Cons:
- No live capture; the briefing has to be recorded elsewhere first
- Hour-capped subscriptions add up for frequent briefings, with extra hours at $10
- Built around transcription and translation rather than structured brief drafting
6. Fathom
Fathom provides a real choice between bot and bot-free capture within the same app, with bot-free currently in beta and limited to Mac. As with Notta’s standard Bot-Free approach, neither mode is local processing, so audio is still uploaded to Fathom’s cloud. For teams focused primarily on capture, its Free plan is unusually generous: unlimited recordings, transcription and storage plus instant AI summaries. More advanced summary capabilities begin at Premium, and account-wide Ask Fathom is a beta with limited lookback on team calls. CRM behavior also needs careful reading: basic sync is capped at three users per domain, while field sync, Deal View and coaching metrics require Business.
Features:
- Unlimited recordings, transcription and storage on all plans including Free
- Basic CRM sync capped at 3 users per domain; field sync, Deal View and AI scorecards on Business
Pros:
- Bot-free capture even on the Free plan, which is rare
- Strongest free tier here for unlimited recording and storage
- Field-level CRM sync on a qualifying plan goes beyond a basic notes push
Cons:
- Bot-free capture is a Mac-only beta, not a mature cross-platform option
- No local or offline processing; both modes upload audio to Fathom’s cloud
- The three users per domain cap on basic CRM sync constrains team rollout
What to Look for in an Audio-to-Text Tool for Client Briefings
Capture flexibility. Briefings happen on video calls, in person and as existing recordings, and a tool covering only one forces a workaround for the rest.
Confidentiality, not just visibility. Keeping an extra participant off the call is a different guarantee from keeping audio off a vendor’s cloud, and sensitive briefings may need the stronger one.
Structured output over a raw transcript. Look for decisions, requirements and action items rather than searchable text.
Cross-briefing memory. Requirements from an earlier briefing are often relevant to the current one.
Multilingual accuracy, including whether mixed-language conversations are supported at all.
Cost structure that matches briefing volume. Per-seat subscriptions, credit-metered AI and pay-per-hour transcription suit different volumes.
Teams whose briefings routinely span all three formats benefit most from a tool that covers all three, which is where Notta is particularly well positioned, especially when a Privacy Mode level of assurance is required.
Frequently Asked Questions
Do I need a bot-free tool for client briefings specifically?
Not always, but it reduces friction. Some clients accept a visible AI notetaker; others find it distracting or disallowed by policy. Having a bot-free option avoids renegotiating the setup meeting by meeting, and most tools listed here now provide one.
Is bot-free capture the same as private or confidential capture?
No. Bot-free simply means no additional participant joins the call. Audio can still be uploaded to a vendor cloud for transcription and AI processing, which is how Granola, Fathom’s bot-free mode, Fireflies’ Desktop App and Notta’s Bot-Free mode all work. Only a local, offline mode such as Notta’s Privacy Mode, on supported plans, platforms, models and languages, keeps audio off the cloud.
What’s the difference between a transcript and a brief?
A transcript is a record of what was said. A brief is a structured account of what was decided and what matters next: the objective, requirements, decisions and next steps, organized so someone who missed the meeting can still act. Most tools here can produce transcripts; fewer can reliably turn a briefing into a brief without manual rewriting.
Closing Take: Choosing an Audio-to-Text Tool for Real-World Briefings
For a single predictable kind of briefing, a tool built around one capture method can be enough: Fireflies when integration coverage is the priority and cloud processing is acceptable, Granola when bot-free virtual calls are the main requirement, Sonix or Descript when the briefing is already recorded and needs to become a clean transcript or an edited deliverable.
In practice, client briefings do not stay that tidy. They happen on calls, in person, and sometimes arrive as a recording captured by someone else. Notta supports that reality within one product across all three capture methods and adds Privacy Mode, a local option none of the other tools in this comparison match. With Notta Brain drafting a structured brief and recalling prior meetings instead of starting from a blank transcript each time, it remains the most complete fit for teams whose briefings are varied in format and sensitivity.

articles.title: Nothing Headphone (1) Pro : le nouveau rival de l'AirPods Max mise sur un design fou, mais divise sur le son
articles.text:

| Coussinets détachables | Oui |

| Expérience utilisateur |  |

| Bluetooth multipoint | Oui |

| Applications | iOS, Android |

Fort d’une expérience encore jeune mais réussie sur le marché des casques, Nothing passe à la vitesse supérieure. Son Headphone (1) Pro pousse chaque curseur : architecture à trois transducteurs, ANC renforcé, confort retravaillé et expérience logicielle enrichie. Le tout sans trop faire exploser la facture…
En plus d’un an, Nothing en est à son troisième modèle de casque sans fil. Après le Headphone (1), qui marquait son entrée sur ce segment, et l’abordable Headphone (a), le fabricant britannique revient avec son casque le plus avancé. S’il ne s’écarte pas de l’ADN visuel de la marque, le Headphone (1) Pro entend repousser l’expérience avec une architecture sonore à triple driver, un confort optimisé et une réduction du bruit promettant 5 dB d’atténuation supplémentaire en moyenne.
Il se distingue aussi sur le plan logiciel en introduisant une fonction d’émetteur Auracast pour partager son signal avec une pléthore de récepteurs compatibles, ainsi qu’un égaliseur paramétrique plus précis. Si l’expérience semble toujours complète, espérons que Nothing soit parvenu à conserver une signature sonore au moins aussi réussie que celle du Headphone (1), malgré l’absence du spécialiste KEF aux commandes du réglage tonal.
Le Headphone (1) Pro est sorti en septembre 2026 à 349 € dans des finitions noir et argent.
Le Headphone (1) Pro a été testé avec la version 1.01.49 de son micrologiciel et l'app Nothing X en version 3.8.2.
Au même titre que la déclinaison allégée Headphone (a), le Headphone (1) Pro ne dépayse pas puisqu’il reprend le design atypique du Headphone (1). Les différences structurelles relèvent du détail avec des coques et un arceau légèrement plus larges, ainsi que des coussinets et un bandeau plus moelleux.
Toujours non pliable, le Headphone (1) Pro se distingue par ses coques rectangulaires en aluminium d’excellente facture, prises en sandwich entre les coussinets et une excroissance transparente, signature visuelle de Nothing. Au sein de cette dernière, on ne retrouve plus de motifs en relief évoquant vaguement une cassette audio, mais l’arrière des chambres acoustiques, visible en profondeur.
Si cette conception se montre plus pertinente, on salue aussi l’usage d’un verre épais plutôt que d’un Plexiglas. Là où ce dernier était incrusté dans la coque du Headphone (1), le verre vient ici la recouvrir jusqu’à ses bords, donnant à l’ensemble un aspect plus abouti. Un vrai gap côté design, qui réduit la perception de l’assemblage. Autre bonne nouvelle, les coussinets sont enfin amovibles au profit de la durée de vie du produit.
Côté accessoires, le Headphone (1) Pro abandonne la fine housse en feutre pour une boîte en plastique qui recouvre uniquement les coques, à l’image de celle de l’AirPods Max 2. Bien que cette solution ait le mérite de mieux protéger les transducteurs que celle d’Apple, ses 383 g se font trop sentir dans un petit sac, d’autant plus par rapport à une housse semi-rigide standard. De plus, elle ne laisse aucune place aux câbles mini-jack 3,5 mm et USB-C, pourtant inclus.
Bien que son poids baisse de 329 g à 327 g, malgré un design légèrement plus musclé, le Headphone (1) Pro demeure l’un des casques sans-fil les plus lourds du marché. Seul l’Apple AirPods Max 2 étant vraiment plus outrancier sur ce point, il se fera difficilement oublier lors de marches soutenues.
Malgré cela, grâce à une bonne répartition du poids, le Headphone (1) Pro demeure confortable. Il procure même des sensations plus agréables que ses petits frères grâce à des coussinets mieux rembourrés et un bandeau un peu plus étendu et épais. S'il se ressent encore un peu sur le haut du crâne, il se montre moins pinçant autour des oreilles, sans que cela n’impacte son excellent maintien. Il n’atteint pas non plus la discrétion de références comme le Bose QC Ultra Headphones (Gen 2) ou le JBL Tour One M3, mais l’effort est notable.
Sur la forme, si le casque hérite du bandeau de l’abordable Headphone (a), on apprécie qu’il ne reprenne pas sa matière caoutchouteuse qui a tendance à tirer sur les cheveux. Par ailleurs, si ses coques ne sont pas des plus profondes, les plus grandes oreilles apprécieront la reconduction des renforts en mousse.
À quelques détails près, le Headphone (1) Pro reprend les commandes de son cadet. Nothing conserve donc l’une des interfaces les plus complètes du marché, entièrement composée de boutons physiques intuitifs. Un capteur de port, d’ailleurs plutôt réactif, est intégré à la coque droite pour gérer automatiquement la lecture lorsque le casque est ôté ou remis.
La molette Roller pilote le volume, la lecture et les modes d’isolation, tandis que le curseur Paddle sert à changer de piste ou répondre aux appels. L’alimentation et la connexion Bluetooth reposent toujours judicieusement sur deux commandes distinctes, tandis qu’un sélecteur Flat s’ajoute au tableau. Celui-ci active un égaliseur censé offrir un rendu “neutre”, réglé par les ingénieurs du Metropolis Studio de Londres. Placé sur la partie supérieure des coques au même titre que le bouton dédié à l’appairage, ce dernier est particulièrement minuscule et difficile à repérer au doigt.
On retrouve aussi le bouton personnalisable, configurable pour deux actions au choix, parmi lesquelles l’assistant vocal, la coupure des micros, le déclenchement d’une photo ou d’une vidéo à distance, ou encore l’accès au carnet de notes intelligent Essential Space sur un smartphone Nothing. Dommage que l’accès à une égalisation préférée ait disparu.
Au même titre que celui de ses petits frères, le récepteur Bluetooth 6.1 du Headphone (1) Pro est particulièrement complet et moderne. Au-delà d’une connexion remarquablement rapide, il prend en charge le codec LDAC pour une réception sans perte avec les sources Android compatibles, les protocoles d’appairage rapide Fast Pair et Swift Pair, sans oublier la gestion des appareils connectés en multipoint via l’app Nothing X.
S’il ne s’agit pas de LE Audio à proprement parler, le Headphone (1) Pro va plus loin que ses petits frères en autorisant non seulement la réception d’un flux Auracast sans appairage classique, mais aussi sa diffusion. Habituellement réservée à Android, cette technologie permet ainsi au casque de partager son audio avec une multitude de récepteurs compatibles, même lorsqu’il est connecté à un iPhone. On regrette toutefois que le mode de diffusion dégrade considérablement la qualité sonore.
La latence native atteint 225 ms, mais peut être réduite à environ 140 ms grâce au mode basse latence. Un gain appréciable, même si la connexion filaire reste à privilégier pour le gaming. Celle-ci se montre d’ailleurs particulièrement complète avec une restitution lossless via USB-C, quelle que soit la source, ainsi qu’une entrée mini-jack 3,5 mm. À noter que le casque ne peut pas être utilisé en passif (éteint) et que l’app n’est plus accessible lorsqu’il est connecté en filaire.
Au sein de l’app Nothing X, la principale nouveauté réside dans un égaliseur paramétrique entièrement revu. Il passe d’une part de 8 à 12 bandes, tout en présentant les fréquences et niveaux avec encore plus de précision. On peut aussi entrer le gain manuellement, ce qui est plus pratique qu’un simple curseur vertical, ou encore profiter d’une fonction bypass permettant de comparer rapidement le rendu avec et sans égalisation.
Outre la gestion de la réception et de la diffusion en Auracast, l’introduction de cinq modes d’audio spatial, l’expérience est aussi complète qu’auparavant (mode basse latence, son personnalisé en fonction de l’audition, localisation par alerte sonore, etc.). Globalement, il faut saluer la fluidité et la réactivité de cette app.
Nothing ne fait jamais rien comme tout le monde, et cela s’étend désormais à une conception acoustique non seulement inédite pour elle, mais aussi pratiquement jamais observée dans l’univers des casques audio.
Au lieu de confier toute la reproduction à un seul transducteur, le Headphone (1) Pro en utilise trois, chacun spécialisé dans une partie du spectre sonore. On retrouve ainsi un transducteur large bande de 40 mm utilisé pour les basses et la première partie des médiums, ainsi qu’un transducteur dit “de précision”, chargé d’assurer la transition avec un tweeter xMEMS qui gère les plus hautes fréquences.
Ce type d’architecture nécessite un réglage très fin pour éviter les pics ou creux aux fréquences où deux transducteurs se chevauchent, phénomène fréquent qui tend à entraîner un surplus de brillance très clivant. Comme on pouvait s’y attendre du fait du transducteur dédié à l’aigu, le Headphone (1) Pro distille un son beaucoup plus expressif et coloré que son cadet le Headphone (1), qui présente certes des basses un peu accentuées, mais des médiums naturels, ainsi qu’un aigu à la fois contenu et détaillé.
Lorsque le mode Flat est désactivé, le Headphone (1) Pro cherche à délivrer un rendu impressionnant, à la fois profond et détaillé, axé sur le sub, mais hélas surtout sur l’aigu. En effet, en sortie de boîte, toutes les fréquences au-dessus de 6 kHz dominent les médiums au prix d’un caractère scintillant. Les sibilances vocales sont exacerbées et perçantes, tandis que les charleys et les cymbales sont à la fois trop présents et fluets.
Les basses surjouées compensent relativement bien cet excès d’aigu en apportant de la profondeur et du corps. L’équilibre n’est pas non plus irréprochable, étant donné que la pente plutôt irrégulière vers le bas-médium ne favorise pas les composantes graves des voix. Celles-ci apparaissent alors souvent un peu plus aiguës que nature. Bien sûr, il n’est pas rare que ces extrémités du spectre envahissantes relèguent les nappes et autres éléments énergiques au second plan. Regrettable, car le niveau de tranchant offert par un haut-médium non surjoué est plutôt transparent.
Si ce réglage tonal a été conçu en interne, cette fois sans l’aide de KEF, le Headphone (1) Pro met à disposition un mode Flat, censé “supprimer la coloration”. Celui-ci atténue le grave en creusant encore davantage le haut-médium pour prévenir toute agressivité, tout en conservant l’accentuation dans l’aigu. Il en résulte un rendu plus naturel des voix, moins réverbérant et inutilement aigu, ainsi qu’un grave mieux contrôlé, mais au prix d’un manque de tranchant rédhibitoire qui impacte la présence des caisses claires et autres éléments incisifs. Malgré cela, les charleys continuent d’être particulièrement fluets, tandis que les sibilances restent accentuées, bien que moins agressives.
À noter que ce mode Flat désactive l’accès à tout l’égaliseur, ainsi qu’au mode Transparence, bridant alors étrangement les fonctions du casque.
La meilleure option semble donc être de jouer avec l’égaliseur paramétrique pour atténuer les basses et l’aigu. Hélas, malgré sa précision, toute atténuation bride un peu le volume général. Cela dit, un égaliseur plus simple permet d’atténuer des régions plus larges, mais celui-ci se limite à seulement 3 bandes… Intégrer de bons égaliseurs n’excuse donc en aucun cas une restitution déséquilibrée en sortie de boîte.
Le système de réduction du bruit du Headphone (1) Pro s’appuie sur 10 micros, contre six sur le Headphone (1), associés à une isolation passive optimisée grâce à des coussinets en similicuir double couche et une nouvelle paroi en silicone conçue pour limiter les fuites. Nothing promet ainsi une atténuation supérieure d’environ 40 % sur l’ensemble du spectre sonore.
À la mesure comme en pratique, l’amélioration est sensible avec près de 20 dB d’écart autour de 200 Hz par rapport au Headphone (1). Le casque se montre notamment beaucoup plus efficace pour atténuer les voix et leur intelligibilité, un point faible de son prédécesseur. Dans un open space, il parvient donc à créer une sensation de bulle. Dans la rue, il excelle également jusqu’à ne laisser filtrer que les composantes médiums les plus présentes du bruit de moteur d’une voiture qui passe.
Le Headphone (1) Pro conserve toutefois quelques faiblesses face aux meilleurs du marché. La réduction démarre assez tardivement, ce qui laisse encore passer certains bruits statiques (ventilations, ambiances urbaines) et ceux de nos propres pas. Surtout, les grondements très graves de certains véhicules, comme ceux d’une moto puissante ou d’un poids lourd, semblent exacerbés. Un phénomène étrange, mais non rédhibitoire au regard de l’excellente atténuation sur le reste du spectre.
Le Headphone (1) Pro réalise aussi des progrès tangibles du côté de la transparence. Le rendu demeure assez peu aéré, tandis que les sifflantes et les sons les plus énergiques manquent de détail. Néanmoins, le système est plus efficace qu’auparavant grâce à une suramplification de la région des 1 à 2 kHz. Les voix conservent ainsi une très bonne clarté et une excellente intelligibilité, ce qui permet non seulement de tenir une conversation dans toutes les situations, mais aussi de donner l’illusion d’une restitution naturelle. Le résultat n’atteint pas celui des Apple AirPods Max 2 et du Sony WH-1000XM6, qui font mieux dans l’aigu, mais reste convaincant.
Si le Headphone (1) Pro multiplie les micros dédiés à l’ANC, il utilise toujours quatre micros pour les appels, associés au traditionnel algorithme Clear Voice. De fait, en milieu urbain bruyant, la captation est aussi médiocre que sur son aîné. Notre voix est restituée de façon distante et totalement voilée, tandis que le passage d’un véhicule bruyant suffit à faire passer certains mots à la trappe.
Dans un environnement contrôlé, le kit mains libres est pleinement utilisable et restitue une voix claire et détaillée. Seuls demeurent perfectibles la qualité du signal, parfois robotique, ainsi que les artefacts audibles en arrière-plan.
Pour son Headphone (1) Pro, Nothing reste vague en promettant plus de 30 h d’autonomie avec l’ANC activé. À 60 % du volume, il a tenu très exactement 37 h 40 min. De très bonnes performances qui le placent juste au-dessus de la moyenne du marché, mais en deçà de celles de ses frères Headphone (1) et Headphone (a), qui ont affiché respectivement une autonomie de 40 h 45 min et 75 h dans les mêmes conditions.
Le Headphone (1) Pro jouit de vrais progrès côté ANC et confort, tout en héritant des bases solides de son aîné en matière de construction, connectivité et fonctions logicielles. Ces qualités suffisent à en faire un très bon casque, même si les appels demeurent médiocres en milieu bruyant et que l’autonomie est en légère régression.
Côté sonorité, la précision globale est au beau fixe. Dommage qu’il cède à une coloration typique des produits à multiples drivers. Là où le Headphone (1) se démarquait par sa restitution naturelle — merci KEF —, ce modèle présente une forte accentuation des basses et aigus, au prix d’un rendu plus scintillant et artificiel en sortie de boîte. Le mode Flat ne parvient pas vraiment à sauver les meubles, ce qui amènera sans doute les auditeurs exigeants à jouer avec l’égaliseur.
Pour justifier un écart de 150 € avec le Headphone (1), il aurait fallu que les améliorations tangibles en matière d’isolation et de confort s’accompagnent d’une restitution sonore au moins aussi équilibrée. Ce n’est malheureusement pas le cas.
À 349 €, le Headphone (1) Pro peine également face à des références comme le Sony WH-1000XM6 ou le Bose QC Ultra Headphones (Gen 2), non seulement en raison de son rendu très coloré, mais aussi d’une praticité en déplacement perfectible (poids élevé, conception non pliable). Il n’en reste pas moins une solution de choix pour ceux qui recherchent un casque original, durable, ainsi qu’une expérience complète et moderne, et qui n’auront pas peur de mettre les mains dans l’égaliseur.

articles.title: El ansiado AVE al País Vasco afronta su reto más descomunal: levantar siete viaductos en apenas siete kilómetros
articles.text:
A las localidades de Manzanos (Álava) y La Puebla de Arganzón (Burgos) las separan menos de seis kilómetros a recorrer en menos de 10 minutos por una apacible carretera. Pero cuando el objetivo es conectarlas con un tren que circula a más de 200 km/h, esa pequeña brecha se puede convertir en un acantilado.
Ese es el reto que tiene por delante Adif AV, encargada de supervisar uno de los mayores problemas de ingeniería al que se enfrenta la alta velocidad Burgos-Vitoria.
Un nuevo tramo. El Ministerio de Transportes ha confirmado la adjudicación para la construcción del tercer tramo de la línea de alta velocidad Burgos-Vitoria a través de Adif AV. Para sacar el tramo se invertirán 241,6 millones de euros pese a que sólo tiene una longitud de siete kilómetros.
Las vías se extenderán entre las localidades de Manzanos (Álava) y La Puebla de Arganzón (Burgos). O más bien podríamos decir casi que "sobrevolarán" porque el verdadero reto está en cómo llevar el tren de una a otra localidad.
Siete viaductos para siete kilómetros. Y es que en su anuncio, el Ministerio de Transportes destaca que el verdadero reto está en los siete viaductos que hay que construir para llevar el tren de uno a otro lado. Pese a que la extensión del tramo es de apenas siete kilómetros, serán necesarios siete pasos elevados para poder salvar todos los obstáculos que hay en el camino.
En total, el tren estará "sobrevolando" el suelo durante 2,5 kilómetros. Es decir, el 35% del tiempo que el tren circule por este punto lo hará sobre uno de estos viaductos. Teniendo en cuenta el tamaño de la infraestructura, veremos una concatenación de viaductos en muy poco espacio.
El más complicado. De todos ellos, uno destaca por encima del resto. Pese a que la suma total de viaductos medirá 2,5 kilómetros, sólo uno de ellos extenderá las vías por las alturas durante más de un kilómetro. Es el más complejo de los siete porque tiene numerosos obstáculos que salvar.
UN VISTAZO A...
Y es que esta infraestructura llevará las vías a 5o metros de altura y se sostendrá sobre un arco de hormigón de 222 metros. El objetivo es salvar de una sola vez el río Zadorra, la línea de ferrocarril convencional Madrid-Hendaya, la carretera nacional N-1 y la autovía A-1 que discurre paralela.
Un pasito más. Este tercer tramo adjudicado forma parte de los siete en los que se han dividido el tramo de alta velocidad Burgos-Vitoria para conectar esta línea con la Y vasca. De momento, de los siete tramos, Transportes destaca que ya hay cuatro en construcción, contratados o en licitación, sumando un total de 54,8 kilómetros.
De esos cuatro tramos en los que ya se trabaja, el primero en construcción, el Pancorbo-Ameyugo, también es muy complicado ya que el 77% de los 8,4 kilómetros discurren a lo largo de los tres túneles y tres viaductos que completan este paso. Además, se han hecho las primeras gestiones para la Variante Ferroviaria de Burgos y Valle de las Navas, de 16,7 kilómetros. En este caso se suceden otros seis viaductos más.
¿Para cuándo? Es lo que no está claro y es que no hay una fecha cerrada para la apertura del enlace de alta velocidad entre Burgos y Vitoria. El objetivo no está definido aunque José Antonio Santano, secretario de Estado del Ministerio de Transportes, apuntaba este mismo año a que espera que la línea esté lista "en cuatro o cinco años".
Y es que las dificultades técnicas son mayúsculas en este paso. Además de las obras ya mencionadas, el proyecto se ha retrasado en algunos puntos. Por ejemplo, en Piérnagas (Burgos) se firmó un contrato para ejecutar las obras en 34 meses. Sin embargo, en 2025 se tuvo que ampliar el plazo de ejecución en otros 15 meses dadas las dificultades y este mismo año se ha vuelto a ampliar el tiempo previsto en otros seis meses porque el terreno es demasiado inestable.
