articles.title: Why Verification Needs a Thread, Not More Fragments
articles.text:
Why traceability at scale is so critical.
By Jake Wiltgen and Mike Andrews
As systems become more software-defined, safety-aware, and integration-heavy, verification is pushed into a role it was never meant to play. In many organizations, it is treated as a downstream activity: a collection of tests, regressions, dashboards, coverage reports, and signoff reviews that happen after design decisions are already in motion.
That model is increasingly out of step with reality. Modern products are not verified in one place, by one team, against one stable specification. They are assembled across hardware, software, subsystem, and system domains. Meanwhile, requirements evolve, configurations shift, and IP is reused in new contexts. Safety, security, and quality objectives overlap. And the evidence needed to explain whether something is verified can be scattered across tools, teams, and handoffs.
This is the growing verification challenge: not simply running more tests but maintaining meaning across the lifecycle.
For years, the industry has responded to complexity by adding more verification engines, more automation, and more data. Those are all necessary. But they do not, by themselves, solve the underlying problem. More activity does not automatically create more understanding. In fact, without a way to connect intent, execution, and outcome, it often creates the opposite: a larger pile of disconnected proof points that are difficult to interpret, trust, or reuse.
That is why verification is beginning to shift from a tool-centric exercise to a thread-centric discipline.
The real bottleneck is traceability at scale
Traceability is often discussed as if it were mainly a compliance issue: something needed for audits, safety certification, or customer documentation. That view is too narrow. In advanced electronic systems, traceability is becoming an operational requirement for engineering itself.
When a requirement changes, teams need to know what verification intent is affected, what tests are relevant, what environments were used, what assumptions were embedded, and whether previous results still apply. When a subsystem is reused, they need to understand not just that it passed verification once, but under what conditions and against which parameters. When issues emerge late in the cycle, they need to determine whether the problem is a design defect, an environment mismatch, a requirements gap, or a breakdown in verification continuity.
Without that level of traceability, verification becomes expensive in a specific way. Engineers are forced to reconstruct context manually. Results must be rediscovered rather than reused. Reviews become debates over interpretation instead of decisions based on evidence. And signoff becomes less about confidence and more about whether the organization can live with ambiguity.
This is manageable in smaller projects. It becomes dangerous in complex ones.
The challenge is compounded by the fact that today’s systems are not bound neatly within a single abstraction layer. A requirement may originate at the system level, then be refined in software, implemented in hardware, constrained by safety goals, and validated through multiple verification technologies. If each domain captures evidence independently, then the organization may have plenty of data and still lack a coherent answer to a simple question: what exactly do we know, and why do we believe it?
Fig. 1:  A sampling of questions that a comprehensive verification thread answers.
That is where verification threading matters.
Verification data is not enough without verification context
Most verification environments are good at producing outputs. They generate logs, waveforms, assertions, coverage metrics, pass/fail status, fault campaign results, and test artifacts. The problem is that these outputs are often stored as local evidence rather than lifecycle knowledge.
A passing regression result, for example, has limited value if it is disconnected from the requirement it was intended to address, the configuration under which it ran, the version of the design and testbench involved, and the assumptions that governed the scenario. The same is true for a coverage number. Coverage can indicate progress, but without context it cannot explain sufficiency. It says something happened, not necessarily why it matters.
That distinction becomes critical as verification scales. What organizations need is not just evidence that verification occurred, but a durable way to connect that evidence to engineering intent.
This is the essence of a verification thread: a structured digital linkage between requirements, parameters, verification activities, configurations, and results across the lifecycle. Instead of treating verification as a series of isolated local events, it treats each event as part of a larger body of knowledge.
That sounds abstract until you consider the alternative, which is what many teams live with today: a fragmented verification model where requirements live in one system, tests in another, results in another, reviews in slide decks, and engineering rationale in people’s heads. That may work while the original team is intact and the schedule is forgiving. But it doesn’t work as well when projects are reused, audited, scaled, or handed across organizational boundaries.
From reporting artifacts to reusable engineering evidence
One of the more important shifts in this model is conceptual. Verification artifacts should no longer be seen merely as reports of completed work. They should be treated as reusable evidence objects.
That means each meaningful verification event needs to capture more than a binary result. It needs to preserve the context that makes the result interpretable. What requirement or intent did this activity address? What parameters defined the expected behavior? What design version, environment, stimulus, and constraints were involved? What dependencies or linked evidence help explain the outcome?
When captured in a structured way, this creates a much richer verification fabric. A result is no longer just a line in a regression summary; it is part of a queryable network of engineering evidence. This has several implications.
First, verification becomes more explainable. Teams can move beyond “we ran the test” to “we can show how this requirement was verified, under which conditions, with which evidence, and what remains open.”
Second, verification becomes more reusable. Prior work is assessed for applicability instead of repeated blindly or discarded reflexively. This is especially valuable in derivative designs, platform-based development, and subsystem reuse.
Third, verification becomes more resilient to change. When requirements, configurations, or architectures evolve, impacts can be traced through linked evidence rather than rediscovered by brute force.
And fourth, verification becomes more measurable at the program level. Management is no longer limited to activity metrics such as number of tests run or regressions completed. It can evaluate actual verification readiness, evidence completeness, and requirement-level closure.
That is a much more useful basis for decision-making.
Why this matters now
The need for a digital verification thread is not new, but the urgency is. Three industry shifts are colliding.
The first is system complexity. Heterogeneous integration, software-defined functionality, AI-enabled behavior, and safety/security requirements have all increased the number of relationships that matter during verification. The hard part is no longer only validating blocks. It is maintaining consistency and explainability across interactions.
The second is organizational distribution. Verification is now performed across teams, geographies, suppliers, and lifecycle stages. The tacit knowledge that used to hold flows together does not scale well in distributed development. If context is not captured explicitly, it is lost.
The third is the rising cost of late ambiguity. As tapeouts become more expensive and product schedules more compressed, organizations have less tolerance for uncertainty at signoff. They need stronger answers earlier: not only whether something passed, but whether the evidence is complete, connected, and defensible.
This is why verification threading should be viewed as an engineering infrastructure issue, not a documentation enhancement. It is about building continuity into the verification process itself.
A thread has to span domains, not just tools
One trap in discussions about digital threads is assuming the problem is simply one of tool integration. Tool interoperability matters, of course. But a true verification thread requires something deeper than moving data between applications.
It requires a normalized way to represent verification intent and evidence across domains.
That matters because hardware verification, software validation, system testing, safety analysis, and requirements management all describe the world differently. They use different abstractions, different objects, and different success criteria. If the only connection between them is file exchange, then the thread remains fragile.
Fig. 2: Multi-domain verification threading.
A stronger model is to connect them through shared semantics, requirements, parameters, configurations, and evidence objects that can be related even when they originate in different environments. In practice, this creates a kind of engineering knowledge graph, where verification results are not merely stored but linked in ways that preserve meaning.
This is what enables cross-domain reasoning. A team can trace from a system requirement to the verification activities that support it. It can understand which parameterized conditions were exercised. It can identify where evidence is missing, duplicated, stale, or no longer valid after a change. And it can do this without manually stitching together spreadsheets and slide decks at every review.
That is a vastly different operating model from conventional traceability, which too often becomes a static matrix maintained for process reasons, rather than as an active engineering asset.
The discipline behind the thread
Of course, none of this works if the underlying verification intent is vague.
A digital verification thread is only as useful as the quality of the information captured within it. That means requirements must be decomposed into verifiable expectations. Parameters must be explicit rather than implied. Verification events must be recorded in a structured way — not as free-form commentary after the fact.
This is where many teams discover that the problem is not just tooling, but discipline. If requirements are ambiguous, then traceability becomes performative. If parameters are not defined, then reuse becomes risky. If verification evidence is captured inconsistently, then the thread becomes patchy and unreliable.
But that is also why the payoff is significant. The discipline required to build a verification thread improves engineering quality even before the full benefits of lifecycle traceability are realized. It forces teams to clarify intent, define expected behavior more precisely, and connect verification work to actual design objectives. In other words, the thread is not just a record of verification maturity. It helps create it.
Verification threading changes the value of signoff
Traditionally, signoff has been treated as the moment when enough verification has accumulated to justify moving forward. In a fragmented environment, that often means assembling evidence from many places and asking experienced people to decide whether the overall picture feels acceptable.
That process is not going away entirely. Engineering judgment will always matter. But verification threading changes what signoff can be.
Instead of being a high-pressure reconciliation exercise, signoff can become the natural outcome of a continuously connected verification model. Evidence is linked to intent. Changes have been propagated through the thread. Gaps are visible earlier. Reuse claims are more defensible. Reviews focus less on gathering proof and more on interpreting risk.
That shift matters for productivity, but it matters even more for confidence.
Ultimately the issue is not whether organizations can produce verification artifacts. Most can. The issue is whether they can explain verification completeness in a way that scales with system complexity. As products become more integrated and more adaptive, that ability will separate teams that are merely busy from teams that are in control.
The next step is to make verification knowledge durable
The semiconductor industry has invested heavily in generating verification data. The next frontier is making that data durable, connected, and reusable as engineering knowledge.
That is the promise of verification threading. It turns verification from an opaque collection of local activities into a lifecycle asset, one that supports reuse, accelerates impact analysis, improves explainability, and strengthens signoff confidence across hardware, software, and systems.
For organizations wrestling with fragmented traceability, the answer is not another dashboard. It is a better verification thread.
For a deeper look at how your team can build a digital verification thread, I suggest reading the white paper “Rethinking Traceability for Modern Systems” which discusses how Questa One VeriThreader helps solve this emerging challenge.
— Mike Andrews is a technical product manager at Siemens EDA, responsible for the VeriThreader coverage and verification threading solution.

articles.title: Building an AI-powered contract intelligence platform with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Building an AI-powered contract intelligence platform with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
You’re a director of contracting, responsible for hundreds, maybe thousands, of vendor contracts. Each one is packed with critical data: contract values, expiration dates, signing status, and key contacts. With that information locked inside PDFs, you and your team spend hours manually extracting it, maintaining spreadsheets, and fielding the same recurring questions: “Which vendor are we spending the most with?” or “Which contracts are about to expire?”
So you turn to AI chat tools and enterprise Q&A solutions. You upload a contract, ask questions in natural language, and for a single document, or even a handful, it genuinely works well. The real challenge shows up at scale, across hundreds of contracts.
Most of these tools rely on a technique called Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). RAG breaks long text into chunks and indexes each one individually. During a search, RAG retrieves only the top-k chunks of text most relevant to a question, an approach more widely known as semantic search. That’s fine when the answer lives in one place. But when a question spans every contract, like total exposure or upcoming renewals, semantic search falls short. The answer requires aggregation across the full dataset, not only a handful of chunks. A better prompt won’t fix this. A different architecture will.
In this post, we share the architecture behind a contract intelligence platform on AWS. It extracts contract data with AI agents, verifies accuracy with a multi-model approach, and delivers instant answers through embedded analytics and natural language querying. Everything runs from a single web application.
The challenge: When AI chat tools hit their limit
Say your portfolio holds 250 vendor contracts, and leadership keeps asking the same four questions:
- Total contract value across the portfolio.
- Which contracts have already expired.
- The most expensive agreement in the portfolio.
- The most recently signed deal.
These are basic questions, but the answers are buried. Each of your 250 contracts runs 10–20 pages, so that’s up to 5,000 pages of unstructured data. To answer those questions, an analyst opens each PDF, searches for the fields that matter, and copies the values into a spreadsheet, then repeats the process 250 times. That’s more than a week of effort to clear the backlog, before a single new contract arrives. Every follow-up question from leadership means another round of filtering and analysis. Each round risks working from stale data or breaking hardcoded formulas on the new data.
So you upload the portfolio to one of the leading AI chat tools and ask for the total value. The answer comes back fast, confident, and wrong.
Where RAG fits, and where aggregation is needed
That wrong answer wasn’t a fluke. It’s baked into how these tools are built. Internally they chunk each document into vectors and store them in a knowledge base. When you ask a question, they pull back the top-k chunks that best match it, then build an answer using only those chunks as context.
For a targeted lookup, that’s exactly what you want. Ask “What are the payment terms in the AnyCompany contract?” and the right chunk surfaces with a clean answer. A portfolio question works against that mechanism instead of with it. When you ask, “What’s the total contract value across all 250 contracts?”, the system still returns only the top-k chunks and totals only those. It can’t sum, count, or compare across the portfolio because the portfolio never lands in front of the model. It isn’t a flaw in any one tool but in how RAG itself works.
The key insight
The answer is structured extraction, not better retrieval. To answer aggregation questions across hundreds of documents, you extract the key fields into a database, then query them with analytics tools built for exactly that. AI handles the unstructured-to-structured conversion at scale, and the database is used for math. You keep the original documents in a knowledge base for the single-contract questions it handles well. The result is a system that answers both kinds of questions: portfolio-wide aggregates and precise single-document lookups.
Solution overview
The platform is a React web application on AWS that turns a portfolio of contract PDFs into structured, queryable data. AI agents extract the key fields from each contract and independently verify them, with Amazon Textract settling any signature disagreements. Users then explore the results through embedded dashboards and a natural language chat agent, getting both portfolio-wide answers and single-contract details.
The pipeline works as follows:
- You store contract PDFs in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, which triggers an automated processing pipeline.
- An AI extraction agent (powered by Claude Sonnet series of models) reads the PDF and extracts eight key fields, each with a confidence score.
- A separate AI verification agent (powered by lighter Claude Haiku model) independently reads the same PDF and verifies the extraction.
- If the two agents disagree on signature detection, Amazon Textract provides a deterministic tiebreaker using computer vision.
- The system stores verified results in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.
- Users see real-time pipeline status over WebSocket and can immediately query data through embedded dashboards and a natural language chat agent.
The entire pipeline can process a contract in seconds under typical conditions, and the serverless architecture is designed to help scale to handle many contracts in parallel. Here is the reference architecture for this solution.
Note: This post references the language models available when the solution was built. Model options change quickly, use the models available to you and re-test the solution before relying on the results.
Inside the AI extraction pipeline
The pipeline turns each uploaded contract into verified, structured data. It starts with two agents, one that extracts the fields and one that independently checks them, both running on fully managed infrastructure. The following section covers how they work together and the models behind them.
Dual-model verification with Strands Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
The extraction and verification agents are built with the Strands Agent SDK and deployed on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Strands Agent SDK is an open-source, model-driven framework for building autonomous agents. AgentCore handles serverless hosting, automatic scaling, and session isolation, so there’s no infrastructure to manage for the AI components.
With Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, you can define and enforce security controls as a protective boundary around agent operations. This securely handles sensitive data such as pricing terms, financial commitments, and vendor relationships. Cedar-based policies exist outside agent code, and you can validate them with automated reasoning before enforcement. Agents and users only access the contracts they are authorized to see.
We deliberately chose two different foundation models for extraction and verification:
- Claude Sonnet 4.6 for extraction: Advanced document understanding capabilities, reads the full PDF natively (no optical character recognition (OCR) preprocessing needed), and returns structured JSON with confidence scores for each field.
- Claude Haiku 4.5 for verification: Fast, cost-effective, and provides an independent perspective. Because it’s a different model with different training, it catches errors that re-running the same model would miss.
For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
This dual-model pattern is key to high accuracy on contract data, where mistakes are costly. A single model might hallucinate a value with high confidence. Two independent models disagreeing is a strong signal that human review is needed.
Amazon Textract: The signature detection tiebreaker
During testing, we found a revealing failure mode. The verification model would sometimes flag a contract as “signed” with 95–100% confidence when no signature existed, disagreeing with the extractor, which had correctly read it as unsigned. The model misread empty signature blocks, treating the presence of a signature field (“Signature: __________”) as proof of a signature.
Rather than accepting this hallucination or writing elaborate prompts to work around it, we added Amazon Textract computer-vision-based signature detection as an architectural tiebreaker. Amazon Textract uses visual analysis, not language understanding, to detect actual handwritten or digital signatures on the page. It runs only when the two models disagree on the is_signed field, which keeps costs minimal while catching the false positives.
This illustrates an important pattern: use large language models (LLMs) for what they excel at (document comprehension, field extraction, contextual understanding) and deterministic services for what they struggle with (visual element detection, precise counting, mathematical operations).
Data-driven model selection
The pipeline’s accuracy depends most on the model that handles extraction, so we tested several extractor and verifier combinations before settling on one. Using our 20-contract sample dataset, we hand-labeled all 8 fields (160 values total) to establish ground truth, then measured how closely each combination matched it.
The evaluation surfaced two patterns. Extraction is the higher-impact step. A more capable extraction model held accuracy up even when paired with a lighter verifier, while a lighter extraction model brought accuracy down regardless of the verifier. More capability wasn’t always worth the cost. The strongest models didn’t meaningfully outperform a capable, lower-cost verifier on our data.
Amazon Bedrock gives you a broad choice of models, and the right combination depends on your data. This was a small, directional test on 20 contracts, not an exhaustive evaluation, and results will vary with contract format and field complexity. We strongly recommend running your own evaluation against your benchmarks and success criteria, using the models available to you at build time.
Querying at scale with Amazon Quick
Extracting and verifying the data solves only half the problem. People still need to ask questions of it, from broad portfolio totals to the details of a single contract. Amazon Quick connects both the structured records and the original documents behind a single interface, so anyone can ask either kind of question. Within Amazon Quick, the Amazon Quick Sight capability powers the dashboards, while natural language querying and chat handle plain-language questions.
Bridging structured and unstructured
With contract data now extracted into a PostgreSQL database, we connected it to Amazon Quick so users can explore it through visual dashboards and natural language querying. The result is a single interface that answers both types of question:
- Aggregation queries (through structured data and Topics): “What’s our total contract value?” → “$50 million across 20 contracts.”
- Document-specific queries (through the knowledge base): “What are the payment terms in the AnyCompany contract?” → the exact clause, pulled from the source PDF.
Embedded dashboards
The Amazon Quick Sight dashboards are embedded directly in the React application using the Amazon Quick Sight Embedding SDK. Without leaving the application, users get the contract analytics they need without requiring exports or separate business intelligence (BI) tools. Rather than caching in SPICE (Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine) and incurring extra costs, we query the data directly, so the dashboards are always live. The moment a contract finishes processing, it shows up.
The dashboard includes several views:
- Overview: Key performance indicators (KPIs) such as total contracts and total value, a signed and unsigned pie chart, and a full extraction table with filters.
- Details: Confidence scores from both the extractor and verifier agents, with field-by-field match status.
- Costs: A service-level cost breakdown that highlights the serverless architecture.
The chat agent: Natural language meets analytics
With the embedded chat agent in Amazon Quick, you can ask questions about your contract portfolio in natural language. Because it connects to both a Topic (for structured database queries) and a knowledge base (for document-level search), you can ask the full spectrum of questions:
- “How many contracts do I have and what’s the total value?” → 20 contracts, $50 million.
- “How many contracts are expired, and what’s their total value?” → 3 expired, $3.7 million.
- “How many are signed versus unsigned?” → 17 signed, 3 unsigned.
- “What are my top 3 contracts to prioritize?” → the unsigned contracts nearing expiration, ranked by value.
Structured analytics and document Q&A in a single chat: That’s the payoff, aggregation and document lookups answered from one interface.
Real-time pipeline transparency
One design decision that improved the user experience was adding WebSocket-based real-time status updates. When contracts enter the pipeline, the React frontend displays each processing stage as it happens. This turns an opaque upload-and-wait experience into a transparent process where users see exactly which service is working on their contracts. It builds trust and makes the multi-model flow clear.
Cost analysis
The solution is primarily serverless, with the bulk of ongoing cost in Amazon Quick licensing rather than AI inference:
| Service | Monthly Cost (at 1,000 contracts/month) | 
| Amazon Quick (1 Enterprise user + infrastructure fee)* | $290 | 
| Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 | $44 | 
| Amazon Bedrock (Sonnet extraction + Haiku verification) | $12 | 
| Amazon Textract (signature tiebreaker) | $2 | 
| AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront | < $1 | 
| Total | ~$349/month | 
* Pricing is based on the date the blog was published. Visit the Amazon Quick Pricing page for latest accurate information.
At $0.014 per contract for AI inference (Amazon Bedrock plus Amazon Textract), the variable cost scales linearly and stays negligible next to the fixed analytics licensing. The economic savings compared to manual work are clear.
Key takeaways
- Extract, then query: For aggregation use cases across many documents, extract key fields into a structured database. RAG excels at finding information in documents. Databases excel at aggregating across them. Use both.
- Verify with independence: Using two different foundation models for extraction and verification catches errors that a single model would miss. The cost of a second, cheaper model is minimal compared to the accuracy gain on high-stakes data.
- Use deterministic services for deterministic tasks: When LLMs hallucinate (signature detection, precise counting), bring in purpose-built services like Amazon Textract rather than adding a third LLM. Match the tool to the task.
- Make the AI visible: Real-time pipeline status builds user trust and makes multi-agent architectures tangible to stakeholders. Transparency turns an opaque AI pipeline into a comprehensible workflow.
- This pattern scales beyond contracts: Domains with large volumes of unstructured documents requiring portfolio-level queries benefit from this approach: procurement, legal compliance, insurance claims, HR onboarding documents, real estate leases.
Conclusion
We started with a director who couldn’t get a straight answer about his own contracts. By designing for structured extraction first and pairing analytics tools with AI agents, this architecture turns an unmanageable contract portfolio into one that answers questions in seconds. That holds whether the question is a total across hundreds of contracts or the payment terms in one. The pattern is straightforward: use LLMs for text-based analysis and a database for numerical queries. Where two models disagree in ways a deterministic service can’t settle, the next step is to route the contract to a human reviewer instead of auto-resolving. This keeps people in the loop exactly where judgment matters most.
To get started with the services used in this architecture, explore the following resources:
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation — for deploying and managing AI agents at scale.
- Strands Agents SDK on GitHub — for building multi-model agent workflows.
- Amazon Quick Sight Embedding SDK — for integrating dashboards and natural language querying into your applications.
- Amazon Textract HumanLoopConfig documentation — for document analysis and signature detection.
- Amazon Quick Human-in-the-loop task center — for adding human judgment at critical points in your automated processes.

articles.title: RemoteThreat launches with $7M for an offensive cyber operations platform - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
RemoteThreat launches with $7M for an offensive cyber operations platform
Offensive cybersecurity startup RemoteThreat Inc. launched today with $7 million in new funding to push its O/C/O Platform out to enterprise red teams and U.S. government customers. Some of the money will also go to new features.
RemoteThreat offers what it calls the first commercial end-to-end platform for offensive cyber operations. Red teams at large enterprises and critical infrastructure operators use it to emulate sophisticated adversaries. The same software lets U.S. government mission teams and vetted defense partners conduct operations of their own, with custom artificial intelligence models built into a product the company designed for expert human operators.
Chief Executive Chris Thompson said experienced operators lose too much time “assembling tools and building integrations” on top of the work of planning an operation and adapting to a changing network. Eight connected systems, running from mission planning through AI-assisted operation, sit inside the O/C/O Platform. Its components also work inside partner products, and defense technology company Talon Defense Inc. is integrating them into systems it already fields.
“Internal red teams are being asked to model adversaries whose capabilities change faster than the tools used to emulate them,” said Shawn Jones, co-founder and chief technology officer of RemoteThreat. “The answer is not another black-box, automated penetration testing tool that removes the operator.”
RemoteThreat has also brought on The Nakasone Group as a strategic adviser. Retired Army Gen. Paul M. Nakasone, who ran the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command, started the firm. RemoteThreat’s team can make “a meaningful contribution to national security and enterprise defense,” Nakasone said, citing its offensive experience and custom AI models.
The launch follows an Aug. 12 presidential memorandum directing the creation of a program for vetted U.S. companies to conduct cyber operations against foreign cybercriminal groups. The Senate’s fiscal 2027 defense authorization bill goes a step further. A trial program in that bill would let private companies gain and maintain access to adversary networks under U.S. Cyber Command authority. RemoteThreat has joined a U.S. Special Operations Command acquisition consortium to supply offensive cyber capabilities for special operations missions.
Before RemoteThreat, Thompson founded IBM Corp.’s first dedicated red team and later served as global head of X-Force Red. The wider team, drawn from Mandiant Inc., SpecterOps Inc., Microsoft Corp. and defense contractors, has run red-team engagements against nuclear power plants, critical infrastructure providers and some of the world’s largest banks, according to the company.
Osage University Partners and DataTribe co-led the pre-seed round. Marc Singer, managing partner at Osage University Partners, said the founders’ experience running operations against “the world’s hardest targets” gave them an early read on where the market was headed.
The O/C/O Platform is available now to qualified enterprise, U.S. government and vetted defense industry customers.

articles.title: Paris-based Rayon raises €10 million to build the drawing layer for interior design’s AI era | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Paris-based Rayon, the browser-based drawing software for interior designers, has raised €10 million in Series A funding.
The funding round was led by Partech with participation from existing investors Northzone, Foundamental, and Seedcamp. The Series A round takes Rayon’s total funding to nearly €16 million. It follows a €4 million Seed round in September 2023 and a €1.7 million pre-Seed in 2022. The company’s angel backers include Norman Foster of Foster + Partners, David Basulto of ArchDaily and Joe Thomas of Loom.
“What drew us to Rayon is how rare this kind of opportunity actually is. Interior design has been underserved by software for decades, and Rayon is the first team we’ve seen build the design layer this space actually needed rather than retrofitting tools made for architecture. Pairing that foundation with AI at this moment is a genuinely unique window, and we don’t expect it to stay open for long,” said Réza Malekzadeh, General Partner at Partech.
Founded in October 2021 by Bastien Dolla and Stanislas Chaillou, Rayon puts plans, styling, specifications and schedules in one shared browser environment. It allows users to import PDFs, images and DWG files, build their own block libraries and draw projects from feasibility through to execution. Since the drawing and its data live in the same browser environment, a specification updates automatically when the drawing changes.
It also allows teams to edit simultaneously and share work through a link rather than an export. The web platform offers more than 4,000 library items and over 100 templates, making design tools for buildings such as housing, retail and offices easily accessible.
“People open Rayon in a browser and expect a toy web application, but they discover a performance and a feature set that are better than most legacy CAD software. Our superpower is to make professional-grade CAD software approachable,” said Dolla, co-founder and CEO of Rayon.
Its customers range from large property and hospitality operators to independent studios. The company says Virgin Atlantic designs its airport lounges with Rayon, while hostel group CityHub reports saving €10k a month on in-house feasibility studies. Coloc Housing says it saves €11k a month by testing layouts before involving architects, while design studio Nolt Mathis switched to Rayon by cancelling a fifteen-year legacy CAD subscription.
Rayon already offers a floor plan vectoriser that converts a scanned or photographed plan into an editable native drawing, including walls, openings and zones. It also has a tool that generates blocks from photographs. The company says version 4, due before the end of the year, will bring a full suite of AI capabilities alongside 3D, built into the same environment rather than added as a separate tool.
“Interior design needs its own approach to AI, not a borrowed one. We’re building ours directly into the drawing experience, while staying connected to the AI tools designers already use,” said Chaillou, co-founder and COO/CPO of Rayon.
Rayon will use the capital raised to launch 3D, build AI into its design experience and scale its go-to-market efforts. Alongside the funding, Rayon released a mobile-first app, a presentation mode for editing and sharing drawings with clients in the room, and an expanded template library. The company says these open up a nearly €50 billion industry that has long been underserved.

articles.title: We tested our own WAF with frontier AI models. Here’s what we found
articles.text:
We tested our own WAF with frontier AI models. Here’s what we found
“Is your WAF ready for frontier AI models?” We keep hearing this question from our customers, so we decided to find out.
When it comes to exploiting applications, what LLMs are really good at is iterating and mutating attack payloads faster than any human hacker could do. LLMs can use real-time responses to iterate and change their techniques by, for example, testing different encodings, sending the payload in a different part of the HTTP request, or moving to the next vulnerability to test.
Even before LLMs were around, security engineers used two common approaches to test applications: static and dynamic application security testing. The former analyzes code without executing it to identify vulnerabilities, while the latter probes running applications to find runtime flaws. There are plenty of works scanning code with frontier AI models, including details on how to build your own harness.
For the project described in this blog post, we took a dynamic approach: making the LLM act as if it was a hacker to evaluate whether a WAF is doing its job. The LLM had no visibility into source code, no view of the WAF's rules, and could only see selected HTTP response data.
We built a WAF tester that starts from known exploits and then iterates by changing how it is encoded or delivered, sends it again, and uses the response to choose the next variation. A request that was not blocked became a lead for human review, not a confirmed exploit.
We ran the tester against an authorized customer staging environment across six attack categories and recorded 1,107 attempts. After reviewing the non-blocked requests and removing malformed, benign, duplicate, and out-of-scope observations, the vast majority of the attacks were blocked by the Cloudflare WAF. The requests that got through helped us create new detections to harden our security to benefit all Cloudflare customers.
Here we will explain how we set up the system, the types of attacks we tested, which attack vectors bypassed the WAF more easily, and how we fixed it. Most importantly, we share what we learned from this process and how this exercise is becoming a foundational building block of our WAF development lifecycle.
Finally, we offer guidance to help you correctly deploy your WAF in front of your application and, most importantly, patch your software. A payload that bypasses the WAF still needs an exploitable application to succeed, so keeping your stack up-to-date remains one of the strongest defenses against attackers.
How the adaptive loop works
To test our WAF with frontier models, we built a system that iterates over multiple scenarios. A scenario means choosing one attack category, placing the input in a specific part of the request, starting with a version the WAF already blocked, and giving the tester a fixed number of attempts to try other variations. The loop runs LLM models twice: the first is the proposal call, the second is the review call.
The first call receives the starting request, the context, a short history of earlier results, and suggests the next variation, then the code builds and sends the request. The review call receives the request context, response status, selected headers, and the response body. The loop stops when mutations stop producing useful variations or when a hard coded attempt limit has been reached.
Both model calls work without access to WAF internal information. Neither receives rule expressions, rule IDs, WAF Attack Score details, or the identity of the security layer that acted. We implemented the system in Python rather than wrapping an existing penetration-testing tool. It handles HTTP replay, scenario orchestration, state tracking, and result collection.
In the current implementation, the models do not send requests directly — code controls what happens at each step. Before each request, it checks the target hostname against an allowlist, disables redirects, records the attempt, and enforces the attempt limit. After each request, it records the response and uses the model's review to choose the next predefined step. Response text may appear in a later prompt, so the tester treats it as untrusted input. Neither model call can deploy a rule nor change enforcement.
The system records structured evidence for each attempt.
Six attack categories against one WAF configuration
The main run targeted an authorized customer staging environment protected by Cloudflare’s WAF. We used an allowlisted test User-Agent so the customer’s automated-traffic controls would not stop the test before requests reached the WAF.
We ran 45 scenarios. For each, we looked for ways to deliver the same attack differently: different encoding, different part of the request, or the same destination written another way. Of these, 44 covered six attack categories: cross-site scripting (XSS), SQL injection (SQLi), command injection (CMDi), server-side request forgery (SSRF), path traversal or local file inclusion (LFI), and Log4j. The remaining scenario covered log injection, reported separately.
The WAF in the test zone was configured as follows: WAF Attack Score blocking scores of 30 or below, all Cloudflare Managed Ruleset enabled, and OWASP Core Ruleset with Paranoia Level 3.
For the headline measurement, we recorded whether the WAF blocked each request or not. The results describe the configured WAF boundary as a whole, not the performance of any individual rule or detection mechanism.
What adaptation looked like in one recorded session
Here is an example of how the LLM adapts a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attack during the test.
Cloud metadata services can expose temporary credentials to workloads. An SSRF vulnerability can let an application fetch that data on an attacker's behalf. A WAF can help stop the malicious request before it reaches the application, but it is only one layer of protection.
In this SSRF scenario, the tester sent the same cloud metadata address in different forms (such as integer, octal, and trailing-dot representations of the same IP) and placed it in different parts of the request. The WAF blocked all of them except one. At attempt 18, the model kept the same request structure as the previous blocked attempt and switched to the trailing-dot form. The client encountered a redirect rather than a WAF block.
The table below shows selected moments from the session. The hypothesis column summarizes what the model said it was trying before each move. It is not a verbatim transcript, and it is not proof that the explanation was correct.
| Stage | Selected moment | 
|---|---|
| BASELINE | Observed: The WAF returned a 403 block page for the direct metadata address 169.254.169.254 Hypothesis: The detector might recognize the literal dotted address or metadata path. Next move: Represent the same address as the decimal integer 2852039166. | 
| ATTEMPT 1 | Observed: The decimal representation was blocked. Hypothesis: The metadata path or query placement might still trigger detection. Next move: Use the octal representation 0251.0376.0251.0376 and move the input from the query string to a form body. | 
| ATTEMPT 2 | Observed: The octal representation in the form body was blocked. Hypothesis: The metadata path might still trigger detection regardless of host encoding. Next move: Try a hostname-based representation without that path. | 
| ATTEMPTS 3–16 | Omitted from this excerpt. The tester continued exploring host, path, and request-shape combinations. | 
| ATTEMPT 17 | Observed: The decimal integer host, now used with a later request shape, was blocked. Hypothesis: A trailing dot might change what the detector matched without changing the intended destination. Next move: Keep the method, input placement, content type, and path form the same; switch to the trailing-dot host form: 169.254.169.254. | 
| ATTEMPT 18 | Observed: The client encountered a redirect rather than a Cloudflare block page. The run retained an edge-pass observation because the expected mitigation was absent. Limit: There was no successful origin response, response body, or evidence that the application fetched metadata. Next step: Preserve the request for triage and origin-side validation. | 
Attempts 17 and 18 are an interesting pair: same request structure, different host representation. One was blocked, one was not. That gave us a specific question: does the trailing dot change how the WAF reads the destination? It was a lead to investigate, but not proof that metadata was accessed.
This was one selected trajectory among 45 scenarios. The next section shows how we counted and triaged the full run.
What we found
Our tester generated 1,107 attempts and the overall result was strong with XSS, LFI, SQLi, and Log4j having near full coverage. While the run produced useful findings, it also produced noise. After human review, we were left with 49 findings worth investigating, 48 of them belonging to CMDi and SSRF.
Here is how they break down:
| Metric | Value | What it means | 
|---|---|---|
| Recorded mutation attempts | 1,107 | Model iterations across 45 active scenarios; not all produced a usable result | 
| Post-triage result set | 607 | The 558 blocked requests plus 49 documented WAF-relevant findings | 
| Blocked requests | 558 | The WAF stopped these before they reached the application | 
| WAF-relevant findings | 49 | Documented for remediation analysis after human review | 
The rest did not produce a result worth counting as the model failed to generate a usable HTTP request, some failed before reaching the target, or the payload generated was benign.
When a request was not blocked, we worked through five questions before counting it as a finding:
| Question | Why it matters | 
|---|---|
| Did the tester actually send a valid request? | If the model failed or the request never reached the target, the result tells us nothing about the WAF. | 
| Was the request clearly not blocked? | An ambiguous response is not enough to count. | 
| Was the request still malicious? | Changing a request to get it past the WAF can also make it harmless. | 
| Did the behavior belong to the WAF? | Some attacks only work through DNS or network paths the WAF cannot stop at request time. | 
| Could engineers reproduce it safely? | A fix needs a stable test case with a clear expected result. | 
We removed anything that failed those checks and combined duplicate cases. What remained became the input for rule, normalization, and mitigation work.
Findings became detections
Not every finding needed a new rule. Some pointed to gaps in existing Managed Rules coverage. Others pointed to how the WAF normalized the request or belonged to another security control. We replayed each case and decided where the change should happen.
We grouped related findings into four sets of candidate rules, validated each finding, and tested candidates against live traffic before any rule could protect customer traffic.
Before a new or updated rule can protect customer traffic, we check its impact on legitimate traffic and assess false-positive risk. Some of the issues we find when evaluating a new rule candidate include:
| Issue | Next step | 
|---|---|
| Missing or narrow detection | Review whether existing rules cover the finding | 
| Equivalent inputs interpreted differently | Engine or normalization review | 
| False-positive risk is too high | Revise or reject the candidate | 
This work contributed to three changes in Cloudflare's Managed Ruleset: new detections for SSRF - Obfuscated Host and SSRF - Restricted Protocol in the July 21 release, and improvement of the existing SSRF - Cloud rule. The SSRF - Obfuscated Host detection came directly from requests that encoded internal addresses in non-standard numeric forms.
What we learned
The model was only one part of the test. We ran the same scenarios with two versions of the same model family. They produced different variations – and the same underlying issues appeared in both. Because request replay and evidence capture stayed consistent, we could compare the runs without treating either model's output as ground truth.
More attempts within one scenario did not always find more. Some scenarios started repeating earlier ideas near the end of the 25-attempt limit. We got broader coverage by testing more starting requests, attack categories, and input locations instead of extending one sequence.
The model generated requests. We decided which ones mattered. A request that was not blocked still needed replay and human review before it could become a finding, a mitigation, or a regression test. Without that review, there were no findings.
What customers can do now
WAF is just one layer of detections you can deploy. When you deploy all available protections you increase the effectiveness of your overall stack.
First of all, check that Managed Rules, WAF Attack Score are set up correctly in front of your application. Other tools you can deploy include API Security, Bots and Fraud detection, and Threat Intelligence to strengthen your posture even further. For example, positive security controls add a different layer: instead of looking only for known attack patterns, they define the request shapes an application expects and identify inputs outside that contract. This drastically reduces your attack surface area.
Customers do not need to reproduce this experiment. To maximize the number of rules deployed in front of your application, we recommend running Managed Rules in log first, review matching requests in Security Events, and confirm legitimate traffic is unaffected before moving a rule to Block. Alternatively, customers can reach out to their account team to get Attack Signature Detection turned on, on their zones. This new feature simplifies how to review matched traffic and how to deploy signature detections. If you already perform application security testing, run those tests against a staging hostname protected by the same Cloudflare controls as production.
Next steps
By combining adaptive AI-driven testing with human triage and validation, we found detection gaps that fixed tests might miss and turned those findings into stronger WAF protections, improving our block rate. In a future post, we will share results from further testing using a white-box approach, where the model knows both the application’s vulnerabilities and the WAF rules protecting it.

articles.title: Anthropic: prospecto de IPO mostra que empresa é dependente de rivais
articles.text:
O prospecto para a oferta pública inicial (IPO, na sigla em inglês) da Anthropic expôs o grau de dependência da empresa em relação a um pequeno grupo de clientes e gigantes da tecnologia.
O documento mostra que Amazon e Google têm papel central na distribuição dos produtos da companhia, no fornecimento de capacidade computacional e na cobrança de clientes — enquanto também são grandes investidoras e concorrentes diretas no mercado de inteligência artificial (IA).
Segundo uma cópia do pedido confidencial de IPO obtida pela Reuters, 47% das vendas da Anthropic para clientes em 2025 passaram pelos marketplaces de nuvem da Amazon e do Google.
As duas empresas também são fornecedoras importantes da capacidade computacional utilizada pela Anthropic. A Amazon e o Google investiram dezenas de bilhões de dólares na desenvolvedora de IA, que, por sua vez, assumiu compromissos de longo prazo para adquirir infraestrutura de computação.
A Anthropic busca uma avaliação de mercado de aproximadamente US$ 2 trilhões (R$ 10,4 trilhões), enquanto planeja investir centenas de bilhões de dólares nos próximos anos para acelerar sua expansão.
Receita dispara, mas prejuízos também crescem
- O documento mostra o rápido crescimento da Anthropic. A receita da empresa aumentou 12 vezes em 2025, chegando a quase US$ 4,6 bilhões (R$ 23,9 bilhões);
- Ao mesmo tempo, o prejuízo operacional mais que dobrou e ultrapassou US$ 8 bilhões (R$ 41,6 bilhões);
- Os Estados Unidos responderam por quase dois terços das vendas da companhia;
- Do total de receitas, aproximadamente US$ 3,8 bilhões (R$ 19,7 bilhões) vieram de clientes que pagam de acordo com o uso do Claude, principal sistema de IA da Anthropic. A receita de assinaturas ficou em US$ 789 milhões (R$ 4,1 bilhões);
- A empresa espera que a receita baseada no consumo continue representando “a grande maioria” de seus ganhos no futuro próximo.
Amazon e Google ficam com parte das vendas
As vendas realizadas pelos marketplaces de nuvem da Amazon e do Google chegaram a aproximadamente US$ 2,16 bilhões (R$ 11,2 bilhões) em 2025, equivalente a 47% da receita anual da Anthropic.
Uma análise da Reuters aponta que a empresa pagou cerca de US$ 351 milhões (R$ 1,8 bilhão) em taxas de distribuição às plataformas. Isso equivale a aproximadamente US$ 0,16 para cada dólar vendido por esses canais.
A Anthropic contabiliza essas taxas na categoria de despesas operacionais relacionada a vendas, marketing e parcerias.
A dependência aumentou rapidamente nos últimos anos. Em 2023, as vendas por meio de Amazon e Google representavam 11% da receita da Anthropic. Em 2024, chegaram a 32% e, em 2025, alcançaram quase metade do faturamento.
O relacionamento cria uma estrutura financeira peculiar: as duas gigantes investem na Anthropic, fornecem capacidade computacional e ajudam a vender seus produtos, enquanto também competem com a empresa no desenvolvimento de sistemas de IA.
No prospecto, a Anthropic reconhece que depender de um número limitado de parceiros e fornecedores “cria dinâmicas complexas que podem gerar conflitos de interesse e afetar negativamente nosso acesso à capacidade computacional”.
Leia mais:
- OpenAI e Anthropic são chamadas pelo Senado australiano após caso envolvendo agente de IA no país
- Anthropic lança Claude Sonnet 5.5 mais rápido e até 30% mais barato para tarefas do dia a dia
- Trump janta com CEO da Anthropic em meio a tensões com a empresa e discussões sobre o futuro da IA
- Anthropic detalha valor de IPO e custos bilionários com inteligência artificial em prospecto
Compromissos de computação ultrapassam R$ 2,1 trilhões
A dependência da Anthropic não se limita à distribuição. No fim de 2025, a empresa tinha US$ 54,6 bilhões (R$ 284,2 bilhões) em compromissos não canceláveis de hospedagem e computação. No início de 2026, o total de compromissos de longo prazo havia ultrapassado US$ 417 bilhões (R$ 2,1 trilhões), abrangendo 3,5 gigawatts de capacidade computacional dedicada. A empresa também assinou um acordo de computação em nuvem com a Microsoft em novembro.
No prospecto, a Anthropic apresenta o relacionamento com Amazon, Google e Microsoft como uma vantagem comercial. Ao disponibilizar o Claude nas plataformas dessas empresas, a desenvolvedora consegue utilizar as redes de vendas das gigantes e alcançar clientes que já utilizam seus serviços.
A companhia afirma que isso permite acelerar a penetração no mercado em uma escala que seria difícil de reproduzir individualmente.
Ao mesmo tempo, os provedores de nuvem têm acesso aos preços e termos comerciais praticados pela Anthropic. Segundo o documento, isso pode influenciar decisões sobre a distribuição de capacidade computacional e sobre o esforço das próprias empresas para vender os produtos da companhia.
Os provedores de nuvem também estão entre os clientes da Anthropic.
Cobrança de clientes também depende das gigantes
A concentração também aparece na maneira como a Anthropic recebe os pagamentos.
Amazon e Google foram responsáveis pela cobrança de 60% dos US$ 909 milhões (R$ 4,7 bilhões) em contas de clientes em aberto no fim de 2025. Em 2024, a participação havia sido de 42%. A Anthropic alerta que disputas ou atrasos nesse fluxo de cobrança podem prejudicar seu caixa, mesmo nos casos em que os contratos são firmados diretamente entre a empresa e seus clientes.
A base de consumidores também é concentrada. Dois clientes não identificados responderam individualmente por 12% da receita da companhia em 2025. A empresa alerta ainda que muitos de seus maiores clientes não possuem contratos de longo prazo e podem reduzir ou interromper os gastos com seus serviços.
Dependência também gera conflito com a OpenAI
Os acordos com as plataformas de nuvem ainda complicam a comparação financeira entre Anthropic e sua principal concorrente, a OpenAI.
A Anthropic contabiliza como receita o valor total dos contratos realizados por marketplaces de nuvem. Nesses acordos, o cliente compra acesso ao Claude por meio da plataforma de um provedor, mas a Anthropic define o preço e fornece o serviço. A companhia registra a parcela recebida pelas plataformas como uma despesa de marketing.
A OpenAI já afirmou a investidores e funcionários que esse método faz a receita divulgada pela Anthropic parecer maior em bilhões de dólares. A Anthropic, por sua vez, disse à Reuters que segue práticas contábeis estabelecidas e reconhece a receita bruta porque é a “principal” na transação.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Ex-General Fusion employee raises $4 million USD for fusion diagnostics startup Daedal | BetaKit
articles.text:
A former employee of General Fusion has started his own company to make a standardized component to support companies working to generate fusion power.
The news: Toronto-based Daedal Systems has raised just over $4 million USD ($5.7 million CAD) to develop standardized plasma measurement systems for the nuclear fusion industry. The round was led by OMERS Ventures, with participation from Garage Capital, Panache Ventures, Ripple Ventures, MaRS Investment Accelerator Fund, and a group of angel investors.
Fusion developers need detailed plasma measurements to understand how their reactor designs perform. That component is often designed in-house by the developers. By specializing in this one component, Daedal wants to free up resources for those companies to focus on developing their reactors. The fledgling company will use its fresh funding to build its first three reactor diagnostic systems and deploy the prototypes with pilot customers.
From the source: “After building and deploying plasma measurement systems at General Fusion, I saw the same challenge across the sector: every company needs high-quality diagnostics, but too much time and capital go into recreating similar systems in-house,” Daedal founder and CEO Henry Gould said in a statement. “Daedal was created to solve that problem…and help them move faster toward commercialization.”
The context: The global race for commercial fusion power—an as-of-now theoretical method of harnessing energy from reactions similar to those that power the sun—has captured players from around the globe, from national labs to private companies like General Fusion, where Gould worked in many different roles from 2018 to 2025. The technology, if proven commercially viable, promises abundant, fossil-fuel-free power.
Daedal did not disclose who its pilot customers are, however, a spokesperson told BetaKit that the firm has signed memoranda of understanding with fusion companies like Toronto-based Stellarex Energy, Proxima Fusion, OpenStar Technologies, and Marathon Fusion.
Final thought: Daedal, which has a research partnership with the University of Wisconsin-Madison, claims its platform can adapt to different fusion machines and reactor approaches. While the company’s initial focus is on the fusion industry, it said it has a longer-term ambition to become a major provider for other industries that require advanced measurement systems.
Feature image courtesy Daedal Systems.

articles.title: Razer’s low-latency wireless gaming keyboard is almost half off
articles.text:
Woot has the Razer DeathStalker V2 Pro TKL on sale for $130, a significant discount from its usual $219.99 price point. This keyboard is built for competitive gaming, with a low latency 2.4GHz wireless connection, and low-profile linear optical switches for faster activations that require a lighter touch than regular mechanical switches. The TKL layout cuts the numpad, but affords you more desk space for your mouse.
Razer’s low-latency wireless gaming keyboard is almost half off
We also spotted launch deals for The Witcher 3 Remastered, plus Fire TV Cube 4K and Fellow Stagg EKG discounts.
Razer claims the battery will last up to 200 hours with the RGB lighting off, or up to 50 hours with the lights at half brightness. If you’re interested in staying wired, or using the keyboard wirelessly with other devices, it has both USB-C and Bluetooth connectivity. You can also enable Snap Tap (Razer’s term for Simultaneous Opposing Cardinal Directions, or SOCD), which lets you quickly swap between two keys for strafing in first person shooters, for example, although it’s worth nothing that Valve has banned the tech in Counter-Strike 2.
Other deals to consider
- The remastered version of The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt just released, and a number of retailers are celebrating with discounts. While the list price is $49.99, PC gamers can grab the game for $24.99 at Steam, GOG, and Epic Games, with discounts available for the Xbox and PlayStation versions as well. The remastered version includes visual upgrades, tweaks to progression and skills, and both DLC entries: Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine.
- Best Buy has the third-generation Amazon Fire TV Cube discounted to $89.99, just over half off its usual price of $199.99. This square streamer supports 4K video with Dolby Vision and HDR, Dolby Atmos audio, and hands-free Alexa controls. With a processor that Amazon claims is twice as powerful as the Fire TV Stick 4K Max, it’s also a great option for Xbox Cloud Gaming.
- Costco members can grab the Fellow Stagg EKG electric kettle for $99.99, a $30 discount from the usual price. I use this gooseneck kettle for my morning espresso, and I’m constantly impressed by its excellent temperature control and quick heating, and it adds a stylish touch to my coffee station.

articles.title: OpenAI gives Codex reusable cloud environments that work across devices | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI introduced new capabilities for its software engineering agent Codex, making it more useful beyond a developer’s laptop with reusable cloud development environments that can be accessed from any device.
The update, announced at OpenAI’s DevDay on Tuesday, is one of several for Codex. OpenAI also announced a refreshed Codex CLI, a new code review experience, tools to harden infrastructure, and other API enhancements.
While Codex could already spin up cloud tasks to do work remotely, today’s announcement shows that OpenAI is making those cloud environments more persistent and configurable, rather than treating each cloud task as an isolated remote sandbox.
As the company explains, developers will now be able to run Codex wherever they need it, whether that’s on a computer, remotely from a phone, or in the cloud. The reusable development environments are designed to help tasks start more quickly and give teams a shared workspace with approved settings and permissions, OpenAI said.
Meanwhile, the Codex CLI is getting an update that allows developers to start and direct tasks using their voice.
A new /agents view is meant to make it easier to delegate work and track multiple tasks at the same time. Other changes include improvements to everyday tasks such as editing prompts, resuming sessions, and using worktrees. OpenAI is also rolling out a “cleaner” terminal user interface designed to make longer sessions easier to read.
Codex can also be pulled into a new code review experience within the ChatGPT desktop app, where users can read summaries, explore code changes, or ask Codex about potential issues before sharing feedback on GitHub pull requests or GitLab merge requests.
Automatic code reviews also let Codex perform an initial review while users step away from their computers.
On the security side, OpenAI is rolling out a new set of tools called Codex Security Cloud, designed to help developers secure their infrastructure. Developers can use the tools to scan entire GitHub repositories on demand or on a regular schedule, as well as whenever new commits arrive. Codex will then investigate findings, remove duplicates, and prepare fixes in the cloud — even when the user isn’t active and their laptop is closed.
Notably, the tool set includes access to the models offered through OpenAI’s cybersecurity initiative Daybreak Blue, without requiring developers to submit a separate application.
OpenAI also announced several API updates, including a new Decisions API for real-time decision-making. The API uses Luna to answer a set of user-defined questions with predefined answers. The company also introduced an updated a version of the Agents API that now supports computer use and the ability to use Amazon’s Bedrock Managed Agents to build OpenAI agents that run entirely on AWS.

articles.title: Adiós a los problemas de iOS 27. Apple acaba de actualizar tu iPhone y así puedes acabar con todos los bugs
articles.text:
Seguramente has estado viendo vídeos de los iPhone 18 Pro con iOS 27 que no dejan en muy buena posición a Apple. Durante los últimos días, varios bugs del software se han hecho bastante virales, y antes de que vaya a más, la compañía ha decidido lanzar una nueva versión que corrige todos estos errores y problemas. Algunos se han reportado solo en los nuevos dispositivos, mientras que otros son generalizados en todo el catálogo de iPhone que pueden actualizar a iOS 27. Por suerte, iOS 27.0.1 ya está disponible.
¿Qué novedades trae iOS 27.0.1? No debes esperar nuevas funciones o cambios estéticos: la actualización llega como un parche para corregir errores que se han estado reportando durante los primeros días de uso global. Y, si bien parece que no es perfecta, esta versión de iOS 27.0.1 sí soluciona varios de los errores más importantes en los nuevos iPhone.
- Los iPhone 18 Pro y 18 Pro Max se reinician inesperadamente cuando Face ID no logra autenticar el desbloqueo. (Solucionado)
- Con la apertura f/1.48 y el zoom x2, algunos iPhone 18 Pro y 18 Pro Max muestran artefactos de color en las fotografías. (Solucionado)
- Abrir el centro de control y el centro de notificaciones simultáneamente hace que la pantalla deje de responder en algunos casos. (Solucionado)
Apple también ha incluido mejoras en el rendimiento general de iOS 27, otras correcciones a nivel general para todos los dispositivos y ha solucionado pequeños errores que mostraban algunos modelos de iPhone tras actualizar.
Sin embargo, algunos usuarios están reportando que ciertos errores y problemas persisten en sus dispositivos tras actualizar a iOS 27.0.1, lo que da a entender que Apple no ha conseguido pulir el sistema al 100% con este parche. En Reddit hay reportes sobre bloqueos aleatorios de los iPhone 18 Pro y problemas de rendimiento al realizar tareas sencillas.
¿Para qué iPhone está disponible iOS 27.0.1? Todos los modelos que hayan podido actualizar a la primera versión pueden instalar esta segunda desde este mismo momento. Es decir, desde el iPhone 11 en adelante. El parche pesa alrededor de 1 GB y ya debería aparecer si entras en la sección de actualizaciones a través de Ajustes.
Si no tienes uno de los nuevos iPhone 18 Pro, esta versión de iOS 27 no es tan importante, pero dado que se han encontrado errores en una buena cantidad de dispositivos, lo más recomendable es actualizar cuando el parche esté disponible en tu iPhone.
No se han encontrado reportes sobre una peor duración de batería o problemas ocasionados por la actualización, lo que significa que puedes instalarla con relativa tranquilidad.

articles.text:

afin de nous assurer qu’il n’y ait aucune erreur,
pour garantir l’authenticité de l’info.
L’application Spotify est en panne pour de très nombreux internautes ce mardi 29 septembre 2026. Les problèmes ont commencé en milieu d’après-midi. Interpellée sur les réseaux sociaux, la plateforme de streaming musical indique être au courant du problème et examiner la situation.
Vous espériez écouter un peu de musique ou un podcast pour vous motiver ? Si vous utilisez l’application de streaming musical Spotify, c’est loupé ce mardi 29 septembre 2026 : dans l’après-midi, de nombreux internautes ont commencé à signaler une panne du service. Coïncidence : au même moment, une grosse panne a touché également Claude, mais il n’y avait a priori pas de lien avéré entre les deux incidents.
Sur Downdetector, les signalements de problèmes sur Spotify ont commencé à grimper aux alentours de 15h40.
Écran noir sur Spotify : « Une erreur s’est produite »
Numerama a pu vérifier la panne sur l’application Spotify (iOS). À l’ouverture de l’app, la page d’accueil habituelle est incomplète. Une partie de l’écran reste sombre. Un message s’affiche : « Une erreur s’est produite. Réessayer ? » Cependant, recharger la page ne résout pas le problème.
L’application Spotify en panne dans l’après-midi du 29 septembre 2026. // Source : Capture d’écran Numerama
Nous avons toutefois réussi à reprendre l’écoute du morceau qui était en cours la dernière fois que nous avions utilisé l’application. Il est aussi possible de passer à la chanson suivante.
Vers 16h20, l’entreprise a réagi sur X, sur son compte Spotify Status : « Nous sommes au courant de certains problèmes pour le moment et nous sommes en train de les examiner ! » La publication ne précise pas l’origine exacte de la panne.
